title: What’s For Dinner? v. 21.07: It’s Pepper Season! Braised pork with peppers, Swordfish with red pepper aioli, and more… - Daily Kos
content:

			publication. A few Christmases ago some foodie friends sent us a very nice Italian cookbook (see below), with a note in the front about their favorite recipe in the book. It quickly became a favorite of ours, too. It features a mix of peppers – sweet and spicy – so I decided August would be a relevant time to present this recipe along with a couple other things we love to do with peppers. This makes a good dinner for two plus leftovers, and I have always found I haven’t left enough peppers for the second time, so consider increasing the amount (weighed, one time, at 14 oz after coring and trimming and all). We have cooked with the peppers we have, not the specific ones the recipe wants us to have, which we have not yet hunted down. I serve this over soft polenta, pouring/spreading the extra polenta onto a small, oiled tray to chill and fry up the next day. The book in fact suggests making the pork and peppers a day ahead and reheating to bubbling. We have never considered waiting that long 😉 Chop the onion, rosemary, garlic, and anchovies together into 1/4-inch pieces. Coat a 12″ skillet lightly with EVOO and heat over med-high, then add the peppers, plus salt and freshly ground black pepper. Toss lightly to sear for about 2 minutes, then remove. Add a bit more oil to that in the pan, and when it is hot, add the pork, salt and pepper it, and brown well on all sides for about 10 minutes, taking care that “the glaze on the bottom of the pan” does not burn. Halfway through, add the bay, and a minute or two later, the chopped onion mixture, and finish browning the pork over medium heat, making sure to stir enough that the garlic does not burn, while the onion becomes golden brown. Add the vinegar. Simmer it “down to nothing” while scraping up the glaze from the pan. Add back the peppers, plus the water and tomatoes. Adjust the heat and let the liquid bubble slowly, covered, 50 minutes or till the pork is tender, stirring occasionally. Check the seasoning and serve, or refrigerate overnight and reheat to bubbling the next day. Serving over soft polenta is recommended. This is from The Italian Country Table, by Lynne Rossetto Kasper I love grilling/roasting peppers! Red sweet peppers are especially good roasted. You can buy jarred, roasted red peppers if you do not have a grill, but you can also roast them in the oven, I am told, or under a broiler – but not too close. The important thing when roasting your own peppers is to roast them whole, turning as each side gets blackened (just the skin, not the flesh). All the time the peppers spend in the hot oven or over the grill (covered!) the whole peppers are roasting, and this time is essential for them to be done right. Then you put the peppers into a heat-resistant container, where they will sort of steam themselves for about 15 minutes. After that, rub off the outer skins, seed and stem the peppers, and you have a delicacy on your hands. Place in a food processor two medium red peppers roasted as above, peeled, stemmed, and seeded, with 1 Tbsp olive oil and about 3/4 tsp salt [original: 1 tsp – my notes say too much; YMMV depending on your use of the sauce.] This recipe is infinitely useful, but it has a specific origin in Weber’s book Real Grilling, in a recipe called “Eggplant, Prosciutto, and Mozzarella ‘Sandwiches’.” You grill oiled, half-inch-thick slices from a globe eggplant – two per “sandwich” – one on both sides till done (maybe 4 minutes on a side on medium) and the other only on its first side. Turn the half-done slice so it is uncooked-side down, top with a Tbsp [or more] red pepper sauce, then a folded slice of prosciutto, a slice of fresh mozzarella, and then basil and the doubly-cooked eggplant on top. Grill, covered, till the bottom eggplant is fully cooked and the cheese is softened. With your food processor running, drop in two roughly chopped garlic cloves and run till minced. Add two red peppers, as above, grilled, peeled, stemmed and seeded, plus 3 Tbsp fresh lemon juice. Puree. In a small bowl, combine the puree with 1/2 cup mayonnaise, 1/4 tsp Kosher salt, and a pinch of cayenne pepper. Keep refrigerated if you’re not using it immediately, but return to room temperature for the recipe that follows. This aioli recipe is from Weber’s Art of the Grill, in a recipe called “Swordfish Kabobs with Roasted Red Pepper Aioli.” OMG this is so good. One probably both cannot and should not have it often, due to the price and possible mercury accumulation in swordfish, but as an occasional treat, perhaps one could be forgiven. The original recipe is for 2 pounds skinless swordfish, which is a lot – my notes say 1 lb worked for three of us. So I make half the recipe and serve any leftovers for lunch the next day. These are the original amounts, for 2 lb fish. Cut the swordfish into 1 1/2″ cubes, and marinate in the refrigerator for 30 minutes in a mixture of 3 Tbsp olive oil, 2 Tbsp freshly squeezed lemon juice, 1 Tbsp paprika (“preferably Hungarian”), and 1 tsp each chili powder and Kosher salt. Skewer the swordfish and grill over direct, medium heat, turning occasionally, until just opaque, about 5-6 minutes total (covered, always). My notes say, “Jasmine rice went with it perfectly!” The fish is excellent on its own, and so we served it to my father-in-law, who hated peppers, suggesting he try the aioli. He marveled to himself that he was going back for seconds of peppers! You’re getting all my favorite cookbooks in this diary (well, not all, they wouldn’t fit). This is from Pintxos, by Gerald Hirigoyen. Piperade is the kind of all-purpose recipe relegated to the “ingredients” section in the back of the book. Slice one small onion thinly, lengthwise. Core, seed, and cut into lengthwise strips 1 red and 1 yellow sweet pepper. Thickly slice (or crush) 6 peeled garlic cloves. Core and cut into ~ 3/4″ cubes four ripe tomatoes (I measured this to be about a pound). I use my monster 12″ Revere frying pan for this. Heat the pan over med-high, then add 1/3 cup olive oil and when it ripples, add the onion, peppers, garlic, and tomatoes. Cook for about 10 minutes, stirring occasionally (or more often) “until the vegetables have softened and have begun to color.” Remove from the heat and allow to cool, then stir in Piment d’Espelette – my notes say 1 tsp worked – and Kosher salt, perhaps a generous version of 1/2 tsp. This stores in the fridge up to 5 days. First off, this works just as a condiment beside an omelette, sausage, good cheese, meat or fish, or whatever you like. Omelette: Mr pixxer cooked up three eggs with a bit of milk, S&P, then added raclette (a great melty cheese) and at the end, some piperade. He jerks the pan to flip over the omelette. I have never been that brave. Pizza! I tried using up leftover piperade once in a pizza, and I loved it. Mixed mozzarella and parmiggiano, more of the former than the latter, put 2/3 of it onto a slightly pre-baked pizza crust, spread piperade over it, and topped with the rest of the cheese. Easy! Sandwich: Just put it on a sandwich with cheese or whatever else you make sandwiches with. Not peanut butter. Piperade-braised beans with baked eggs: This is a classic, and the recipe is originally from Pintxos. Using the 3 cups (one recipe) of piperade above, 2 cups chicken or veal stock, and 2 cups dried cannellini beans (picked over, rinsed, soaked, drained), plus a 2-oz piece of smoked ham, and two choricero peppers (YMMV – I have not found this particular type), cook the beans for 1 or 1 1/2 hours, or till tender but not mushy. The chef has you discard the ham and choricero peppers but I would for sure eat the ham 🙂 Let cool to “warm”* and preheat the oven to 400. This is enough for six servings, but we make only two of the following, and have the rest reheated later without the eggs. Fill oven proof dishes each with about 1/6 of the bean mixture, make a well in the center of each, and break an egg into it. Place on a rimmed baking sheet or on the oven rack if you are confident you will not spill anything. Cook about 15 minutes, or until the whites are cooked, but the yolks are still soft. Sprinkle with salt and some parsley and serve. [*I have found that you need the beans pretty warm for the egg to cook effectively in them. The beans will be either insulating or cooking the bottom of the eggs.] Here’s one last, lovely pepper recipe from Martha Stewart. This is a GREAT potluck dish in that it’s easy to mix at the last minute. Opposing that…. well, if the definition of “gift item” is “something that looks more expensive than it is,” perhaps the definition of “potluck contribution” should be “something that looks harder than it is.” This is not that, simply b/c it takes a lot of time to cut everything carefully. But then, it’s so beautiful! What’s for Dinner? is a Saturday evening get-together where friends share recipes, talk about good food and help others answer culinary questions. title: Instant analysis of Jaguars preseason performance v. Saints - Yahoo Sports
content: The Jacksonville Jaguars won their preseason opener against the New Orleans Saints by a score of 24 to 20. But this time of the year isn't about wins and losses. In the preseason, individual performances often take priority, with playing time, roles, and roster spots up for grabs. With the clock now at triple zeros, here are our instant takeaways from what took place. - An already banged-up Jaguars' offensive line unit suffered another injury, with Chuma Edoga exiting the game after the first play. - Without Edoga and with the backups in, it was tough sledding for the Jaguars' offensive line for the most part on Saturday. The Saints generated four sacks, six tackles for loss, and seven quarterback hits. - When the Jaguars offense did have some success was at the start of the third quarter when they were able to lean on the run game. That was a nice possession for J'Mari Taylor. The same could be said for Jacksonville's other second-half scoring drive. But otherwise, running the ball wasn't easy. - Ventrell Miller and Branson Combs both saw extended action with the linebacker competition still unfolding. - Speaking of linebackers, I thought Yasir Abdullah had a very good performance, totaling two tackles, a sack, and a tackle for loss. He also helped force a fumble. - Wesley Williams is trying to earn a regular rotational role, and the Jaguars gave him plenty of snaps to boost his stock. - As a collective unit, the Jaguars' defensive front as a whole held up well against the run. - Saints' quarterback Zach Wilson generated several explosive passing plays. Corey Ballentine was picked on a few times. - Throughout training camp, Liam Coen has wanted to test Nate Boerkircher and Tanner Koziol; that continued in this game with both seeing action early. Rookie wide receivers Josh Cameron and CJ Williams saw their share of snaps and targets as well. - Carter Bradley getting the bulk of the snaps tells us that he is very much ahead of Joey Aguilar on the depth chart. That said, it was mostly a rough outing for Bradley. - BJ Green always seems to be around the football this summer. That ability helped him recover a fumble. - Spoiler alert: Cam Little and Logan Cooke are ready for the regular season. - Chandler Brayboy handled kick return duties well. - It's a crowded edge rusher room, but a nice showing from UDFA Bryan Thomas Jr., who had four tackles, one for a loss, a sack and two quarterback hits. - Rookie defenders Jalen Huskey and Albert Regis had good debuts. title: Chesterfield v Fleetwood Town: League Two stats & head-to-head - BBC
content: Veteran striker Ched Evans scored the only goal of the game, finding the net against one of his former clubs to give Fleetwood Town an opening day 1-0 victory at Chesterfield. It was a frustrating afternoon for Chesterfield, who were also beaten by Fleetwood in the Carabao Cup last week. Evans shot narrowly wide from close range and Will Davies saw his effort beaten away by keeper Ryan Boot before the goal, which came in the 35th minute. It was a superb strike, with Evans sending an audacious lob over Boot from around 30 yards out. Lee Bonis went closest to scoring for the home side before the break, first putting a low shot wide and then heading off target from a great position. Lewis McCann threatened to add a second goal, forcing a save from Boot after running at the defence. At the other end, Jay Lynch protected Fleetwood's lead, getting down smartly to save from Fraser Bryden. Chesterfield enjoyed plenty of possession but failed to force an equaliser as the visitors defended resolutely. Both League Two meetings between Chesterfield and Fleetwood Town last season ended 1-1, but the pair haven’t drawn three matches in a row before in the Football League. Fleetwood Town have won just one of their last six away league games against Chesterfield (D2 L3), winning 1-0 in October 2016 under Uwe Rosler. Among sides who were in League Two last season and remain in the division for the 2026-27 campaign, no side were ahead on the scoresheet for a larger percent of their matches than Chesterfield (32.7%). Fleetwood Town netted just 23 goals across their away League Two matches last season, last scoring fewer on the road in an EFL campaign in 2015-16 (19). Timão arrive off a 2-0 league win at RB Bragantino and a 0-0 draw away to Rosario, a run that hints at defensive stability. Kaio Jorge's six league goals underline their edge in the box. Raposa may look to stretch the game, while Corinthians could lean on their compact shape and crossing threat, with 22.98% open-play cross accuracy. A home win could lift Timão and strengthen their Sudamericana push, while Cruzeiro can consolidate a top five berth and their Libertadores second stage pathway with a positive result. title: The GTA RP Server Rockstar Once Fought Is Coming to Its Launcher - GTA BOOM
content: Grand Theft Auto VI is scheduled for November 19, 2026 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S. A chronological look at official reveals, verified leaks and predictions that proved false or remain unverified. Follow trending bets, check your position, and learn how the game works. NoPixel V, the rebuilt NoPixel roleplay server, launches in closed beta on September 8 through the official Rockstar Games Launcher. The most-watched city in Grand Theft Auto is about to move into Rockstar Games' own house as NoPixel V, a full rebuild of NoPixel, the biggest and most famous Grand Theft Auto V roleplay server on the planet, is launching in closed beta on September 8. It will run directly through the Rockstar Games Launch with a launch trailer premier scheduled for September 1 over at nopixel.com. Koil, NoPixel's founder and lead developer, broke the news to the community on Discord and called it a big step for the whole roleplay scene, completing a series of sentences we just wrote that would have sounded absurd as recently as a couple of years ago. NoPixel is the flagship, the server that turned GTA RP into must-watch streaming and kept GTA V culturally alive for years. For almost its entire life, it ran on unofficial tools, living in fear inside a legal gray zone that Take-Two Interactive and Rockstar have long had issues with. NoPixel and nearly every serious RP server were built on FiveM, a community-made framework that let people run their own GTA V multiplayer worlds and once labelled as an unauthorised service that enabled piracy by their eventual owners. Yet, the company that called this stuff piracy is now the one set to host it, right beside Grand Theft Auto Online and Red Dead Online. An officially backed NoPixel V means more stable, more legitimate, and no longer one cease-and-desist away from disappearing overnight. However, it's not all sunshine and rainbows. Putting NoPixel on the launcher legitimizes it and quietly reframes the biggest mod in the scene from an unconfined community experiment into an extension of the official brand, with Rockstar holding leverage it never had over access, rules, and whatever monetization arrives later. Elsewhere, Take-Two shut down alt:V, one of the last independent GTA modding platforms, back in February, and Rockstar has flipped its whole approach to mods from lawsuits to storefront. Clearly, this win comes with an asterisk, which is probably why NoPixel V is taking it easy with its initial launch, keeping its invite-only list exclusive only to roughly 450 creators and established players. With that said, we're far more curious about what this all means for Grand Theft Auto VI and the franchise going forward. We know nothing about modding for GTA 6 and Rockstar will reportedly not talk about its online component for the foreseeable future. In the meantime, there is even chatter that NoPixel V runs on a new in-house framework that could one day retire FiveM altogether, which would put the whole thing under Rockstar's roof end to end. Overall, launching NoPixel V feels like Rockstar's way of keeping the RP streamer economy fed and happy inside its walled garden as it caters to streamers ahead of GTA 6's Netflix premiere on August 27 and November 19 launch. Ray is a GTA BOOM editor and news writer covering GTA 6, Rockstar and Take-Two, GTA Online and franchise history using primary-source reporting. title: Charles V. Bennett - Olean Times Herald
content:
HINSDALE — Charles V. Bennett formerly, of Olean, passed away Tuesday (Aug. 11, 2026) after a long illness. He was born in Udon Thani, Thailand, on March 23, 1973. He was adopted by his father, Guy, and immigrated to the U.S. “Butch” as he was affectionately called by his family, was a 1992 Bradford (Pa.) High School graduate. He went on to attend Pitt Bradford and Houghton College before pursuing a long career at Zippo Manufacturing and later at Luv Toyota dealership. He enjoyed being in nature and had many hobbies. Fishing, hunting, camping, geocaching and riding his motorcycle were just a few his favorites. He enjoyed a fulfilling life of activity and adventure. He is survived by a daughter, Kristin Bennett; two grandchildren, Katai and Raina; sister, Lisa O’Neil; brother, Andy Bennett; stepmother, Karen Bennett; stepfather, Don O’Neil; stepmother, Linda Kemick; stepbrother, James Spitalere; stepsister, Ashley Haynoski; stepsister, Katie Bennett; stepbrother, Ross Bennett; niece and nephews Israel, Judah and Ezra; and many cherished friends. He was proceeded in death by his mother, Chaweewan O’Neil; and father Guy Bennett. A memorial gathering will be held from 4 to 6 p.m. Monday (Aug. 17, 2026) at the Letro-McIntosh-Spink Funeral Home, Inc., 646 E. State St., Olean, at which time a memorial service will be held. The Rev. Bruce Taylor, pastor of Abundant Life Ministries, will officiate. Online condolences may be made at www.letromcintoshspinkfuneralhome.com. title: Rice fall camp notes: ‘slot’ position, linebacker update, Wisne v. NCAA - Underdog Dynasty
content: Scott Abell provides an update on Jesus Machado’s eligibility and a returning player from Wisne v. NCAA. The Rice Owls are three weeks away from their 2026 home opener against FCS opponent Houston Christian, gearing up for year two under head coach Scott Abell. Here are several developments from the Owls’ fall camp practices: Add Underdog Dynasty as a preferred source to see more of our reporting on Google. One position unique to Scott Abell’s gun choice offense is the ‘slot’ — essentially a hybrid running back/receiver role who frequently engages in pre-snap motions. Last season, Aaron Turner held down the role with a team-highs 63 receptions (26 more than anyone else on the roster), 398 receiving yards, and 259 rushing yards. This year, the ‘slot’ position may not be belong to one player. Instead, Rice might turn to a committee. Premier candidates include Virginia transfer Davis Lane, Wake Forest transfer Ben Grice, Holy Cross transfer Max Mosey, and redshirt freshman Colin Leahey. Lane boasts the most FBS experience in the room with 24 appearances at Virginia, where he registered 40 rushing yards on offense and six tackles on special teams. His versatility was a major factor which piqued Abell’s interest during the transfer portal window. “I’m always intrigued by high school quarterbacks,” Abell said. “As I looked on UVA’s roster, he led them in tackles on special teams. He was their third running back and played safety in his career. I’m like, okay, jack of all trades. That’s what our slots are. They’re hybrid guys. They’re running backs, receivers — jack of all trades.” Lane said the Owls’ coaching staff and the opportunity to provide greater impact were significant factors leading him to from Virginia to Rice. There was an adjustment period in learning Rice’s option-based offense — particularly when it came to open-field blocking — but Lane is embracing his expanded role in a new setting. “It’s been an adjustment for sure, but it’s been fun,” Lane said. “The position I’m playing now, you really gotta be a football player to make stuff happen. I’ve enjoyed blocking, running routes, all of that has been fun.” One of Rice’s most significant transfer additions this offseason was seventh-year senior inside linebacker Jesus Machado. Machado suited up for Tulane from 2020-24, posting 40 tackles for the 2022 Cotton Bowl champion Green Wave and a team-high 98 tackles in 2023. However, he suffered a torn ACL in the 2023 Military Bowl, causing him to miss the entirety of the 2024 season. Machado transferred to Houston in 2025 where he reunited with head coach Willie Fritz. In his return from his ACL injury, he played 51 special teams snaps and 15 defensive snaps across four games before entering the transfer portal in October. He committed to Rice in January and was expected to serve as a key contributor in the Owls’ revamped defense. That plan is now on hold. Machado, nicknamed “Zues,” is currently being denied a seventh year of eligibility by the NCAA. He is attempting to receive a redshirt for playing only four games in 2025, after previously receiving a COVID-related redshirt in 2020 and a medical redshirt for missing the entire 2024 campaign. “Right now the Zues situation is out of our hands and Zues’ hands,” Abell said. “We’re preparing to be without him, and we’re preparing to be with him. We knew mid-summer that this was going to be a possibility. We want Zues back. There is no doubt. But it’s out of our hands. So we’re at the mercy of the courts and the NCAA.” Rice, however, has a contingency plan. The Owls added two former Nevada linebackers, Stone Combs and Austin Harnetiaux, during the summer. Combs ranked second on Nevada with 74 tackles last season, while Harnetiaux added 37, and both could assume significant roles on defense, especially if Machado remains unavailable. “We’ve got a lot of guys getting reps,” Abell said. “We were able to add an addition in Stone Combs. We added him into the roster. Austin (Harnetiaux) joined this summer, also from Nevada. So we’ve got answers there.” On July 31, U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney made a ruling that could reshape college football rosters. The verdict of this case, Wisne v. NCAA, extended a fifth year of eligibility to all high school athletes who graduated in the class of 2022. Although the NCAA plans to appeal, the ruling has already prompted several programs — including but not limited to Arizona and UCF — to return previously-graduated players back for the 2026 season. Rice is joining that company. Tight end Micah Barnett, a 2025 team captain, has returned to fall camp in the aftermath of the ruling. According to Abell, Barnett has seamlessly transitioned back into football shape, thanks in large part to his role with the program prior to the ruling. “He was really prepared,” Abell said. “He was with us all summer, interned as a strength intern, so he worked out all summer. He’s a machine. He’s really ready.” Barnett primarily plays tight end and previously lined up at fullback prior to Abell’s arrival. But the head coach hinted that the potential fifth-year senior could see snaps at linebacker, a position he previously played. “I can see him getting a taste on both sides,” Abell said. Ryder Burton waited years for an opportunity. UAB gave him one last October, and now he’s the 2026 starter. title: MATCH REPORT: All Blacks v Vodacom Bulls | Rugby's Greatest Rivalry - All Blacks
content: Revealing more of their intended game plan and extending the selection headaches for next weekend’s Test against South Africa, the All Blacks secured a 50-19 win over the Bulls at Loftus Versfeld in Pretoria to remain unbeaten on the Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry tour. Inspired by a Man of the Match performance from flanker Anton Segner, the All Blacks posted eight tries, as the intensity of their play ran the home team ragged. However, if they had a fault, they did not make the most of the opportunities they created. Segner topped the All Blacks’ tackle count with 13, made 12 carries and secured key turnovers to ensure a consistent supply of quality ball for the backs, where centre Rieko Ioane, wing Leroy Carter and second five-eighths Anton Lienert-Brown thrived in the free-flowing contest. The All Blacks turned on the pressure by moving the ball, requiring the Bulls to make 159 tackles to 127 by the All Blacks, while the Bulls also missed 42 tackles to lead 24-0 at the turn. Ioane relished being back and closer to the action, making 15 carries. Carter popped up all over the field to score two tries and make 16 carries and five line breaks. Lienert-Brown and fullback Beauden Barrett each made 12 carries. Capping the effort, wing Josh Moorby managed two tries and 13 carries. Improvements in conceding fewer penalties (eight) and in unleashing a powerful All Blacks scrum five metres from their line broke an early impasse where both teams attempted to make the most of time in the opposition’s respective 22m areas. The Bulls had a try denied when the ball was short of the line. But they had another chance from the scrum. The All Blacks drove them back, secured a penalty, and cleared the ball downfield; from the lineout, they worked it through the line, through the second wave, and Moorby scored in the 14th minute. The All Blacks ran the restart back at the Bulls with Ioane making 40m down the sideline, but the ball was lost inside and toed ahead by flanker Hanro Liebenberg, who toed the ball downfield and looked to have scored a try, two minutes later. However, a TMO check revealed Bulls fullback Willie le Roux knocked the ball on. Then, a Bulls midfield kick was taken by Barrett, who was unchallenged and ran forward to lob a high kick to Carter, who took the ball on the full and linked with Ioane. The ball was moved wide to No8 Peter Lakai on the left flank. He passed inside for Moorby to score his second try. Le Roux fired a hard pass at close quarters in a Bulls midfield play, and the All Blacks recovered to take the ball deep into Bulls territory. As they pounded the line, retreating Bulls tighthead Francois Klopper was unable to get out of the way of halfback Cortez Ratima’s pass. Klopper was sin-binned and from the resulting tap penalty hooker and captain Codie Taylor marked his return with a 31st-minute try. The Bulls’ mistake rate and inability to make the most of chances resulted in Taylor scoring a second try when the All Blacks were under advantage, after the half-time hooter had blown. Lock Fabian Holland provided impetus for a ruck turnover, which the All Blacks quickly utilised. When the ball was worked towards the line, it was Holland, standing off a ruck, who back-handed a pass that allowed Taylor to charge over for the try. The Bulls stunned the All Blacks in the first minute of the second half when they used a penalty lineout for lock Ruan Vermaak to get a full head of steam on and charge to the line. Referee Nika Amashukeli awarded a try, then overruled the TMO, who said there was no evidence the ball was grounded on the line. The All Black response was instant as they secured the ball off a turnover and moved it across the field for Carter to somehow avoid contact with the sideline to score. A Lakai turnover in the 48th minute saw impressive co-ordination between forwards and backs, resulting in Carter providing a return pass infield for Ioane to score. The Bulls scored their second in the 53rd minute when No8 Jeandre Rudolph set sail at speed down the blindside from a scrum. Linking with first five-eighths Curwin Bosch, they got the ball in the hands of wing Stravino Jacobs, who crashed through Barrett’s tackle attempt to score. Benefitting from the tired opposition, the All Blacks posted 40 in the 66th minute when the ball was released from a lineout maul. Ioane picked up a low pass from replacement halfback Kyle Preston, and while Barrett and first five-eighths Josh Jacomb were both pulled down short of the line, it was Carter who was on hand to take the support pass and score his second. Bulls replacement fullback Hakeem Kunene had an immediate impact after the Bulls called for a scrum in front of the All Blacks posts. He received the ball from replacement halfback Paul de Wet at speed, and his pace took him just short before captain and flanker Marcell Coetzee secured the ball to score. The All Blacks responded by using a penalty to kick to the corner, secure the lineout and launch replacement second five-eighths Timoci Tavatavanawai at the line. He set up clean ball, and the ball landed in replacement No8 Wallace Sititi’s hands for him to score beneath the crossbar. Next up, the All Blacks head to Johannesburg to face South Africa in the opening Test of the series next weekend. Bulls 19 (Ruan Vermaak, Stravino Jacobs, Marcel Coetzee tries; Curwin Bosch 2 con) All Blacks 50 (Josh Moorby 2, Codie Taylor 2, Leroy Carter 2, Rieko Ioane, Wallace Sititi tries; Beauden Barrett con; Josh Jacomb 4 con). HT: 0-24

title: Elizabeth Hurley’s Plunging, V-Neck Swimsuit Is Proof That a One-Piece Can Be “Just as Sexy” as a Bikini - Yahoo News Singapore

While promoting her swimwear collection Elizabeth Hurley Beach, the actress wore a plunging halter-neck design with a low-cut back. Hurley argued that the one-piece swimsuit can be "just as sexy as a bikini" and proved her point with a sun-kissed photo shoot. Celebrities have been bringing the heat all summer long in every variation of bikini imaginable. From cheeky thong bikinis to tiny string bikinis, there's been no shortage of two-piece swimwear inspiration. Elizabeth Hurley, however, is making a compelling argument for the one-piece swimsuit. On August 14, the actress argued that the one-piece swimsuit, which typically features more coverage than a two-piece look, can be "just as sexy as a bikini." "I 🩷 a one piece 🩷 it can be just as sexy as a bikini, sometimes more so," she captioned a photo of herself showing off a plunging, halter-neck design on Instagram. Like Hurley, several famous faces have been spotted rocking the one-piece swimsuit this season, each putting their own special twist on the look. "Life's a beach 💋," she captioned a photo of herself modeling the bikini under a leopard print sarong on Instagram. While her love for swimwear isn't limited to any specific design, Hurley's plunging swimsuit definitely feels like proof that the one-piece can hold its own against a bikini any day. title: Bulls v All Blacks: 5 takeaways as tourists 'ready' for Bok Tests - Planet Rugby
content: Josh Moorby scoring a try v the Bulls with an inset of Anton Segner Following the All Blacks’ 50-19 win over the Bulls in game three of the Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series, here are our five key takeaways. The All Blacks continued their winning run on South African soil with a comfortable 50-19 win over the Bulls, which will leave them brimming with confidence ahead of the upcoming Tests against the Springboks. Eight tries, matching that of their win over the Sharks, were run in across the evening, coming courtesy of braces from Josh Moorby, Codie Taylor and Leroy Carter alongside further efforts from Rieko Ioane and Wallace Sititi. The Bulls did get three of their own, with Ruan Vermaak, Stravino Jacobs and Marcell Coetzee going over the whitewash, but it was mere consolation as the All Blacks had outright dominance on the night. Simply put, this was a performance that showed the All Blacks are ready for the Test series now. They held the front-foot up-front, improved their attack from even their previous outing against the Sharks and overall it just looked like a far more complete performance. It’s a win that shows they are ready to kick on now. Bring on the Tests. Injuries might have put a slight dampener on things, but the All Blacks could not have wished for a better start to their tour of South Africa, especially heading into Test One. Across their three fixtures so far, Rennie’s side have scored a staggering 142 points (an average of 47 points-per-game) and conceded just 40 (13 points-per-game). Elsewhere, a number of players have really pushed their cases for Test selection, some of which might have been thought of as fringe players at the start of it. The obvious caveat to their start is the fact it has come against club sides still very much in pre-season with a number of their key players in the Springbok squad ready for the showpiece Tests, but the All Blacks dispatched of their opponents well. Crucially, they have improved gradually across the series, building on the things and forming a more complete game as a result. Latest World Rugby rankings: Final standings before Springboks v All Blacks confirmed This will put them in good stead looking towards the Tests, which will be some series. If the victory over the Sharks was a sign of things to come, then this win against the Bulls has only solidified that. This All Blacks side, led by Dave Rennie and attack coach Mike Blair, are throwing caution to the wind ball-in-hand and looking to play joue joue, champagne rugby. That is certainly a simplistic, sweeping generalisation of what is actually a pretty intricate, detailed attack, but the point stands. This All Blacks side are here to play fun rugby, and are making that very clear. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. It was almost rugby’s equivalent of tiki-taka football. Offloads, either in and around the tackle or those basketball-esque, were littered across their game, all done with the aim of shifting the point of contact. Pull-backs from the tip of the forward pod out to a playmaker were also a major part of this plan, again just changing the position of attack to create just a bit more space. That then got the likes of Josh Moorby, Leroy Carter, Rieko Ioane and Beauden Barrett, the key game-changers, playing in pockets of broken field where they could just cause havoc for the Bulls defence. Elsewhere, Cortez Ratima’s and Kyle Preston’s desire to inject tempo into the play around the breakdown, often distributing as soon as he arrived, just caught the Bulls off-guard and allowed the tourists to play away when their opponents were still getting back into shape. That only works when the players around him are set into shape themselves, which the All Blacks got thanks to the consistent interchanging between both Josh Jacomb and Barrett at first-receiver. It was very clever half-back play, and was almost organic in its functionality. There’s a saying in rugby that you need to ‘earn the right’ to play wide, mainly by going tight and straight; and the All Blacks certainly did that. Anton Segner again made himself a willing carrier in the ugly areas of the pitch, as he continues to impress on this tour, as did Peter Lakai, Tyrel Lomax and Codie Taylor to name just a few. That combination got the All Blacks consistently over the gainline and consistently on the front-foot, which is exactly when Ratima or Preston would come into their own. Some handling errors were in there, as you would expect with another new 23-man combination, but let’s just call those creases that need to be ironed out rather than completely removed from their system. There’s a lot that both Rennie and especially Blair would have liked about this attack. The All Blacks potentially had two main areas to fix up ahead of the Test series: the scrum and their discipline. Tonight, it seemed they had those issues sorted out. Look, it’s impossible to go through a game without conceding a penalty of any kind, but they conceded far less tonight than in their previous two fixtures this tour, with eight compared to the 16 against the Stormers. Crucially, it was also the areas and the times in which they were, well, not conceded that will please Rennie. Before, the All Blacks would often concede them just as they were getting into scoring position, especially against the Stormers, but that again seemed to have been sorted out and it allowed them to really put a score on. They also conceded them in strings in both previous games, which now also seems a thing of the past. Bulls v All Blacks: Follow the Rugby’s Greatest Rivarly tour match, LIVE The scrum was also much more consistent. Against the Stormers, it was on the back foot for a lot of the game and both front-row units were put under the pump. It was better against the Sharks, but again potentially not consistently dominant across the 80. Tonight, both front-row units seemed to have the better of their opposition, and that will please Rennie no end heading into the Tests. As you would expect with the final round of auditions before the Springbok Tests get underway, Rennie will be left with some real food for thought. Segner again left his mark on proceedings with an immensely powerful display on both sides of the ball. Barrett had a much better run of it than against the Stormers in the opening fixture, which crucially came with 15 on his back. Carter carried on from where he left off in the opener, too, grabbing two tries and an assist as well as being arguably their biggest attacking weapon. Jacomb played with real confidence, which comes amid the backdrop of Richie Mo’unga’s return to the All Blacks set-up. To be perfectly honest, you could go right through the team, the entire 23-man squad for that matter, and say they put themselves in a really good light looking towards Ellis Park. That will leave Rennie pondering, especially with the players he has in the extended touring party, and that sort of horrible headache is exactly what he would have wanted at this stage. title: All Blacks player ratings: Wingers make Dave Rennie's selection job 'incredibly difficult' for Springboks Test while Beauden Barrett hits back - Planet Rugby
content: .All Blacks Leroy Carter and Beauden Barrett. Following the All Blacks’ 50-19 victory over the Bulls in the Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry tour clash at Loftus Versfeld on Saturday, here’s how we rated Dave Rennie’s men. 15 Beauden Barrett: With a cloud around Damian McKenzie’s fitness, Barrett was given a chance to audition for the full-back role at altitude against the Bulls after his struggles at fly-half against the Stormers. The veteran playmaker looked far more comfortable at full-back, injecting himself into the attack wonderfully. He did well to assist Moorby’s first try, timing his pass to perfection, and then played a pivotal role in the winger’s second try too with a superb late chip over the top for Leroy Carter, which got the All Blacks in behind before throwing the long ball out to Peter Laka’i, who provided the assist. He kicked really well out of hand too. After an underwhelming first hit out in South Africa, Barrett hit back in style. 8 14 Leroy Carter: Caleb Clarke’s injury eased the wing selection debate somewhat until tonight. Carter was outrageous from start to finish as he floated around the pitch looking for work and to make an impact. He played a big role in Moorby’s first score with his blistering crossfield run, then crucially reclaimed Barrett’s kick for the second. He did outstandingly well to stay in field for his try early in the second half, assisted Ioane’s before doubling his own tally. He has made it incredibly difficult for the coaching team to overlook him. 9 13 Rieko Ioane: Another who had the opportunity today to play his way into matchday 23 to face the Springboks at Ellis Park, and Ioane did as much as he could. He made great decisions on both sides of the ball, scored a try, and assisted another. His versatility makes him a great candidate for a place on the bench with his ability to cover wing and centre. Question remains: has he done enough? Only time will tell. 8 12 Anton Lienert-Brown: A glue man in the backline again for the All Blacks as he did what was required of him when it was needed with no fuss. While he often took the ball into contact, he still distributed well and was solid defensively. 6 11 Josh Moorby: Like Carter, he has made the All Blacks’ coaching team’s job insanely difficult as they piece together the back-three to face the Boks. He took his try opportunities well and barely put a foot wrong all game. 7 10 Josh Jacomb: First start and boy did he make the most of it with a controlled, level-headed performance. He is unlikely to force his way into the Test team considering the experience of those ahead of him, but Jacomb’s stocks certainly rose at Loftus. He acrobatically stopped Le Roux’s quickly taken penalty kick to catch from going out and hit a wonderful 50:22 too. For the most part, his decision-making was spot on, and he played a real conductor role, not overplaying his hand. 8 9 Cortez Ratima: A decent 40 minutes where he ran great support lines and provided good service to his halfback partner. There were a handful of occasions where he did take the wrong option, but nothing too detrimental. 6 Josh Kronfeld believes Springboks series ‘not super fair’ on Dave Rennie as All Blacks role is a ‘deal for the World Cup’ 8 Peter Lakai: A couple of handling errors aside, it was a strong shift from the Hurricanes man who didn’t hurt his chances of featuring in the Test back-row but didn’t make a compelling case either. Sharp and accurate for his 54 minutes. 6 7 Anton Segner: Another who was clearly pressing his case for a spot in the matchday 23 for the Test matches. The German-born loose forward was aggressive in contact and pitched in with two notable turnovers when the Bulls looked to be threatening the All Blacks. 8 6 Simon Parker: His game is built around his physicality and work-rate and he delivered on both while being a handy lineout option. Parker rarely has a poor outing and today wasn’t one of them, though he will be incredibly disappointed with how slow he was off the one scrum which played a significant role in Stravino Jacobs’ try. 7 5 Patrick Tuipulotu: A solid 50-minute outing from the experienced lock who simply did his job and did it well in all facets of the game. He was part of a pack that won the battle up front – where the Bulls are traditionally strong. 6 Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. 4 Fabian Holland: It was a bit of a weird performance from the lock who was let off the hook by the TMO after finally spotting Le Roux’s knock-on. Holland had charged back to cover Liebenberg’s kick through and looked to have it covered before misjudging his dive on the ball. Ultimately it mattered little, but he also spilt the ball with the try-line begging later in the half. He showed off his slick hands on several occasions, with one particularly good offload sending Codie Taylor through. Still, he had far more good to his game than bad. 7 3 Tyrel Lomax: Part of a front row that utterly dominated the Bulls, issuing a clear warning to the Springboks. A handy distributor and carrier around the park too. 8 2 Codie Taylor (c): Rennie could not have asked for much more from his tour captain today as Taylor issued a statement of intent and proved why he is the first-choice hooker for the All Blacks. He made a great captaincy call to force a scrum right after the Bulls lost Francois Klopper and then added salt to the wounds with his contentious try after his dummy quick tap. He added another five points to his tally and didn’t return in the second half, but he didn’t need to. The coaches saw what they needed to; Taylor was accurate with his lineout throws and part of a dominant scrum. 8 1 Xavier Numia: Along with Lomax, Numia was immense in the scrums, made some good contributions around the park and was hooked at half-time after a job well done. 8 Replacements: A mixed bag from the bench, epitomised by scrum-half Kyle Preston who had good and bad moments. title: Cadillac’s 830-HP V-ONE is its wildest performance concept in 20 years - How-To Geek
content: Cadillac hasn't built a true one-off concept since the Cien debuted at the 2002 Detroit Auto Show, a drivable V12 supercar that hinted at where Cadillac's performance ambitions were headed, right up until the cost of its custom engine and a projected $200,000 price tag kept it from ever reaching production. The V-ONE picks up that same thread, except this time the concept isn't just inspired by racing. It's built from it. Cadillac Design, Cadillac Racing, and chassis builder Dallara developed the V-ONE together. The single-seat concept shares its suspension, transmission, and hybrid V8 foundation with the V-Series.R, the prototype winning races at Le Mans and across the IMSA and WEC calendars since 2023. Plenty of automakers start with a production platform, add a wing, wheels, and graphics, and call the result track-inspired. Cadillac did the total opposite with the V-ONE, starting with actual competition hardware and working from there to build something a single owner could eventually sit in and drive. Although the V-ONE won’t be for sale, what Cadillac is showing here with its debut at The Quail, A Motorsports Gathering, is where the V-Series line could head next. As noted a moment ago, the V-ONE shares its foundation with the Cadillac V-Series.R, the prototype that competes in the IMSA WeatherTech Championship and the FIA World Endurance Championship. Since the V-Series.R debuted in 2023, Cadillac Racing has picked up 10 wins, 16 pole positions, and 32 podiums across IMSA and WEC competition. The stretch includes the 2023 IMSA WeatherTech Championship sweep of the manufacturer, team, and driver titles, a front-row Hyperpole lockout at the 2025 24 Hours of Le Mans, and Cadillac's first 1-2 finish in WEC competition at São Paulo. The V-ONE concept's hybrid drivetrain shares its foundation with the V-Series.R race engine, delivering a combined output of 830 horsepower. The concept also uses the same double wishbone suspension setup as the V-Series.R, with pushrod-actuated coil and torsion spring elements plus lateral and heave dampers front and rear. Meanwhile, the transmission and select electronics also carry over from the race car, while the aero package follows the same proportions that helped the V-Series.R compete at Le Mans and other WEC events. Cadillac's goal with the V-ONE is to keep that race-bred hardware intact while making the car easier and more intuitive for a single driver to operate. This monstrous machine leaves sports cars in its dust. Cadillac's V-Series performance lineage and the idea of a one-of-one build come together in the name V-ONE. Its single-seat cockpit is the first of its kind for the brand, which might be somewhat hard to believe given Cadillac’s racing heritage. Inside, the seat is shaped to the driver's exact measurements, while the steering wheel layout was created with race engineers for actual track use. Instead of a standard infotainment system, the V-ONE uses a race-inspired interface and data visualization system designed to give the driver feedback as they explore the car's limits. Other unique touches inside include recycled fabrics and exposed carbon. As for the exterior, the hand-sprayed paint features a gradient blend from silver to deep navy, meant to reflect the shift from day to night during an endurance race. The concept also gets a new V-Series wheel design, updated V-Series badging, and a serialized plaque on the door. Cadillac is channeling the energy of its racing programs into more than just wildly cool concepts like the V-ONE. To mark its first season on the Formula 1 grid, the automaker built just 26 units of the CT5-V Blackwing F1 Collector Series, a 685-horsepower, manual-transmission sedan developed alongside Formula 1 and the FIA. Likewise, Cadillac gave the F1 Collector Series the same kind of hands-on attention to detail as the V-ONE. Working with their colleagues at GM Motorsports, Cadillac engineers created the most powerful Blackwing to date. The 6.2-liter V8, which produces 685 horsepower and 673 lb-ft. of torque, has an upgraded supercharger with a CNC-machined cover and a laser-etched FIA logo, created in-house by GM Motorsports. Each of the 26 cars is finished in Midnight Stone Frost, a matte black paint that mirrors the Cadillac F1 Team livery. Noteworthy interior details include a 3D-printed F1 shifter medallion and a custom Cadillac Formula 1 door sill plate. Although the V-ONE is not for sale and the CT5-V Blackwing F1 Collector Series was extremely limited, both show the promise of the V-Series lineup. With the V-ONE especially, enthusiasts have a lot to look forward to. "The Cadillac V-ONE Concept is the ultimate manifestation of a customer performance concept and is a clear sign of our ambition for the Cadillac V-Series brand in the future," said Dominic Najafi, Executive Design Director, Global Cadillac. title: Cadillac's V-ONE Concept Proves Its Le Mans Race Car Has Been Sandbagging All Along - autos.yahoo.com
content: Every race car sold to the public through homologation rules is, by design, less than it could be. Regulators cap horsepower, restrict aerodynamics, and standardize hybrid output so a grid of different manufacturers can theoretically finish within a few tenths of each other. Cadillac just handed over the paperwork on how much sandbagging that actually requires. The V-ONE concept revealed on August 14 shares a chassis, bodywork, and V-8 with the Cadillac V-Series.R that races at Le Mans, Daytona, and everywhere in between — and with the rulebook tossed aside, it makes roughly 830 horsepower, well beyond what the actual race car is allowed to produce on a Sunday. Underneath, there's no pretending involved. The V-ONE rides on the same carbon-fiber tub that Italian chassis specialist Dallara builds for the V-Series.R, wrapped in bodywork pulled from the identical molds as the race car. As Cadillac LMDh Propulsion Manager Sean O'Shea puts it, the V-ONE is "about as close to the race car as you can get." The 5.5-liter naturally aspirated V-8 carries over too, hand-assembled in Pontiac, Michigan by technicians who've spent entire careers building race engines, a process that eats up 160 hours per engine before it ever gets bolted into a chassis. That labor bill alone explains why Cadillac has no intention of selling this thing. The horsepower story is the most interesting engineering wrinkle here. IMSA and WEC competition rules cap the combined output of the V-Series.R's V-8 and hybrid system to keep prototype entries from different manufacturers competitive with each other, a form of technical parity that's kept top-tier endurance racing close for years. Strip that ceiling away, as Cadillac did for the V-ONE, and the hybrid motor stops being a compliance tool and becomes a straight-up power adder. Drivers get a push-to-pass-style button that dumps an extra 134 horsepower into the car on demand, the same broad idea behind the boost buttons showing up on hybrid road cars like Audi's own 987-horsepower supercar, just borrowed from a Le Mans pit lane instead of a marketing deck. Cadillac is targeting lap times within roughly 10% of the actual V-Series.R's race pace despite that power advantage, because the V-ONE's hybrid system is intentionally simplified and its aerodynamic package blends elements from multiple V-Series.R iterations rather than a single homologated spec. This isn't simply a race car with a bigger power button. It's a related but distinct aerodynamic and software tune, built around a road-adjacent driving experience rather than a 24-hour fuel and tire strategy. The visual differences matter more than they might seem. Race cars get vinyl wraps because liveries change constantly and repainting a chassis mid-season isn't practical. The V-ONE, freed from that logistical reality, is hand-painted in a gradient that runs from silver at the nose to a near-black "Caspia" blue at the tail, a nod to the light-to-dark rhythm of a long endurance race. It also previews two pieces of future Cadillac hardware: a new V-Series logo and a wheel design the brand says will show up on production V-Series models down the line. Cadillac has been aggressive about building out that performance sub-brand lately, including the 685-hp CT5-V Blackwing F1 Collector Series it built to mark its first Formula 1 season, and the V-ONE reads like the halo-est version yet of that same push. Inside is where Cadillac clearly spent its design budget. The cabin swaps the race car's tight, function-first seat for a GT3-style bucket that trades a bit of snugness for far better visibility, while the steering wheel went through three dozen design iterations before landing on a shape that still carries over much of the actual race car's switchgear. Blue ambient accents echo the exterior livery, and here's the part worth flagging for anyone who assumes concept car means show-car safety: the V-ONE retains the FIA-approved survival cell from the V-Series.R and was validated against the same FIA crash and structural standards as the real race car. That's a meaningfully higher safety bar than nearly any road-going concept ever needs to clear, and it's a good example of how expensive it gets to build "just a concept" when the base architecture is a motorsports-homologated tub. None of this is for sale. Cadillac says so explicitly. So why build an 830-horsepower press vehicle that can't generate a single sales transaction? Because halo cars have never really been about the car itself; they're about what a brand wants people to believe about everything else in its lineup. Cadillac is running two strategies at once right now: reintroducing gas-powered versions of the XT6 and CT5 after leaning hard into an EV-first plan that didn't land the way GM hoped, while simultaneously pouring resources into motorsport-adjacent performance flexes like the V-ONE and its Formula 1 program. A race-car concept that shares its chassis, engine, and now-public design language with a production-bound V-Series wheel is cheap marketing insurance. It tells buyers the brand's performance credibility is real, even while the showroom lineup is in flux. Cadillac's LMDh program has earned pole positions, race wins, and a championship since it returned to prototype racing, exactly the kind of on-track pedigree brands love borrowing for a concept like this. It's the same instinct that sends manufacturers like Honda into Monterey Car Week with two dozen championship-winning race cars just to remind everyone where their engineering comes from. The V-ONE won't turn a wrench for anyone's driveway, but it's a clean look at what a modern LMDh platform can do once nobody's worried about beating a rival manufacturer by exactly the right margin, and a pretty good hint at where Cadillac's next real V-Series street car might borrow its face.

title: Chelsea v Real Sociedad - Chelsea Football Club
content: Morgan Rogers marked his first game in Chelsea colours with a goal and Joao Pedro added to his impressive summer tally by bagging a brace as Xabi Alonso’s Blues ended our pre-season schedule in style. On a sizzling summer’s afternoon in west London, Rogers poked us ahead early on after Joao Pedro’s header had been well saved. Sociedad carried a threat of their own and levelled shortly before the half-time whistle courtesy of Jon Mikel Aramburu’s fine volley. However, the second half was very much Chelsea’s, and our dominance was rewarded through a pair of Joao Pedro goals - his sixth and seventh of pre-season. The well-placed header that restored our lead arrived a couple of minutes into the second half, and the Brazilian backed that up by making a one-on-one opportunity look very easy as this enjoyable friendly entered its final act. Xabi Alonso, getting his first taste of the  home dugout at the Bridge, was able to give minutes to 20 of his players, including several who had yet to feature this pre-season. For the Blues fans watching on, it whet the appetite for what lies ahead, with the start of the Premier League campaign just over a week away now. Before kick-off, Alonso received a great ovation from the Chelsea supporters inside the stadium, and indeed the small pocket of travelling fans who saw him come through Real Sociedad’s ranks in the late nineties. Alonso’s first Stamford Bridge starting XI included new signings Marco Palestra, Maxence Lacroix and Rogers. The latter two were playing their first game for us having returned to training earlier in the week. The shape was nominally 3-4-3, with Pedro Neto and Palestra the wing-backs. Reece James joined Moises Caicedo in midfield, with Cole Palmer and Rogers – as well as Neto and Palestra – supporting Joao Pedro. It was apparent from the off how fluid the attack would be, with Joao Pedro regularly dropping deeper, allowing Rogers and Palmer to run beyond. However, it was from Joao Pedro’s positioning in a central striking position that we took the lead in the tenth minute. Neto teased a cross in from the right flank and the Brazilian’s header back across goal was well directed. Visiting keeper Alex Remiro, diving to his left, just reached it but succeeded only in teeing up Rogers, who couldn’t miss in front of the Shed. Joao Pedro almost immediately forced Remiro into another good save, with nobody in blue able to pick up the pieces on this occasion. Sociedad then threatened for the first time, Ander Barrenetxea cutting inside and curling a shot not far wide. Either side of a hydration break, which offered both teams some respite on another scorching London afternoon, Take Kubo shot into the side-netting and Rob Sanchez produced a superb reaction save to deny Jon Martin. It looked like we had quietened the Sociedad threat sufficiently before the break, but the side from San Sebastian equalised on the stroke of half-time through Arambaru’s brilliantly executed 20-yard volley. Sanchez stood no chance. The Blues came out of the blocks quickly and soon restored our lead, in similar fashion to the opener. Palmer twisted back and forth before laying the ball off for James to send over a right-wing cross. Joao Pedro rose highest and this time his header was steered beyond Remiro’s reach. Another attack involving Palmer ended with the Brazilian firing against Remiro’s legs as the angle narrowed, and there was plenty more slick interplay for the home fans to enjoy as we approached the hour mark. The first ranch of changes saw Mike Penders, Malo Gusto, Josh Acheampong and Enzo Fernandez enter the fray. Gusto went to right wing-back, with Neto switching to the left. One of Sociedad’s subs, Spain World Cup winner Mikel Oyarzabal, had a shot excellently blocked by Wesley Fofana shortly after coming on. But it was our leading man who was more decisive following another flurry of Blues subs – including a first sighting of Pep Chavarria in blue. Gusto played a fine through pass for Joao Pedro to run on to, and the confident finish that followed across Remiro felt inevitable. We continued to look threatening in the final quarter-hour, with Estevao shooting over and Jorrel Hato embarking on a lung-busting run from one end to the other that had the Blues fans roaring him on. It epitomised an enjoyable finale to pre-season. The Premier League season! The Blues begin the 2026/27 campaign by making the short trip to Craven Cottage to play Fulham next Monday 24 August. title: York City v Bristol Rovers: League Two stats & head-to-head - BBC
content: York City were playing their first match in the EFL since May 2016 York debutant Harry Boyes bagged a brace to mark the club's return to the English Football League after a 10-year absence with a thrilling 3-2 home triumph over Bristol Rovers. Boyes – a summer signing from Southend – netted the first EFL goals of his career and was joined on the Minstermen scoresheet by Alex Newby. Clinton Mola had given Steve Evans' visitors a first-half lead and substitute Tommy Leigh later levelled from the penalty spot, but Boyes had the last say for York. A raucous sell-out home crowd were quietened when the Pirates scored from their first attack on the half-hour mark. Keenan Gough's long ball picked out Fabrizio Cavegn on the left and his low cross saw Mola squeeze a shot goalkeeper Alfie McNally. York responded with two goals in four second-half minutes. First, on the hour, Joe Grey's low cross was turned in from eight yards by Newby before Boyes fired home from 15 yards in the 63rd minute. The visitors equalised in the 78th minute after Morgan Williams was controversially penalised for a shove and Leigh sent McNally the wrong way with the subsequent spot-kick. But Boyes headed in from a yard in the 80th minute to win it after Newby had nodded down Ollie Banks' deep cross. Evans: "It's individual errors for each of the goals" York City are winless in each of their last five Football League meetings with Bristol Rovers (D2 L3), since a 4-1 home win in 2012-13. The last time Bristol Rovers started a Football League campaign with an away trip to York City it ended goalless, in the 1971-72 third tier season in which the Gas finished sixth and the Minster Men 19th. This will be York’s first EFL game since a 1-1 draw with Morecambe in May 2016. Overall, they’ve won just one of their last 16 matches in the Football League (D5 L10), though did lose just one of their last six on home soil (W1 D4). Bristol Rovers ended the 2025-26 League Two campaign unbeaten in nine games (W8 D1) and they last went 10+ games unbeaten in the Football League between March and September 2007, a run of 13 ended by Yorkshire side Leeds United. title: The Japanese V-6 Engine So Reliable, The Automaker Still Hasn't Replaced It - topspeed.com
content: Since Japan's introduction to the global automotive market, it has cemented a reputation for    creating engines that are efficient and reliable without sacrificing power. The industry achieved this by adopting traditional manufacturing philosophies that date back hundreds of years. This expertise came into play during its postwar industrial recovery, resulting in Japan becoming a global leader in powertrain engineering. Over the past 70 years, Japanese brands have refined a unique approach that combines extensive quality control with the     use of tried-and-tested technologies. In doing so, these brands ensure that performance gains never come at the expense of long-term durability. This engineering discipline was particularly evident as they expanded into the American premium market, where they introduced sophisticated six-cylinder engines aimed at competing with the region's heavier and less reliable V-8s. Honda is considered one of the leaders in this space, thanks to a well-balanced six-cylinder unit that remains in production today. After a successful initial run in the U.S., Honda began taking its approach to the American premium segment far more seriously. 1986 saw the introduction of the Acura sub-brand, which hit its stride during that same period and into the 1990s. "Precision Crafted Performance" was the primary ethos the brand applied to challenge far more established European and American segment leaders. Reliability and engineering acted as Honda and Acura's trump card, led by the Legend sedan and coupe. These premium midsize models quickly rose to become the best-selling luxury import in the United States for six consecutive years, spanning the late 1980s and early 1990s.     Acura followed this up with the NSX Benefiting from a lightweight, all-aluminum body and VTEC technology, it became an everyday supercar that could outperform the exotics of its era. Today, both Honda and Acura have pivoted toward crossovers and SUVs to align with market trends, but their ethos of doing more with less remains unchanged. In fact, many of the brand's powertrain foundations from the 1990s can still be seen in the vehicles they sell today. Honda's focus in the 1990s centered on powertrain mastery. The Japanese brand applied a philosophy that focused on extracting high power output from smaller-displacement units without sacrificing longevity. The brand achieved this by opting for aluminum components, including lightweight die-cast alloys for both blocks and heads to improve thermal efficiency and lower weight. A key design element was the refinement of variable valve timing and lift, which allowed engines to switch between distinct cam profiles.     Honda's famous VTEC system This dual-mode capability optimized low-end fuel economy for daily commuting and high-RPM airflow for performance. It was supported by racing-derived innovations such as low-friction internal coatings, forged steel connecting rods, and high-precision secondary balancer shafts that virtually eliminated the vibrations inherent in inline four-cylinder designs. Honda went as far as developing its own specialized machining tools to achieve micron-level tolerances, cultivating a bulletproof reputation in the process. These engines were engineered to operate reliably at high rotational speeds that would have caused mechanical failure in many American and European rivals. The Japanese company first introduced this powertrain in the 1997 Acura CL, effectively debuting its J-Series V-6 family. This was Honda's official successor to the C-Series, maintaining a smooth 60-degree V-angle configuration. Its construction utilized a die-cast aluminum alloy block with iron cylinder liners for durability, paired with single overhead cam aluminum heads featuring four valves per cylinder. Honda also opted for a belt-driven valvetrain and a dual-stage intake manifold. Pairing this configuration with the VTEC system gave the engine a broad torque curve and high-RPM breathing capacity that rivaled larger-displacement engines in refinement. Reliability was a fundamental aspect of the development process, made possible by a forged steel crankshaft, high-strength connecting rods, and a simplified cooling circuit that reduced potential leak points. This robust approach to internal components means that the     J30 can easily surpass 200,000 miles with basic maintenance, setting a gold standard for the premium segment by offering a trouble-free ownership experience without sacrificing performance. Honda applied the J30 V-6 to several models that enjoyed considerable success in the U.S. market. The first vehicles to adopt it were the 1997 Acura 3.0CL and the 1998 Honda Accord V-6. Honda also used variations of this engine internationally in the Odyssey Prestige and Absolute trims, as well as the Honda Inspire and Avancier. Depending on the model, the J30 produces from 200 horsepower in the early J30A1 variants to a peak of 244 horsepower in the 30th Anniversary Edition J30A5. The torque range typically spans from 195 to 212 pound-feet. Honda typically mated these engines to four- or five-speed automatic transmissions paired with front-wheel drive, though the 2003 to 2007 Honda Accord V-6 Coupe was available with a six-speed manual transmission to appeal to driving enthusiasts. The engine's legacy was revived in a modernized, turbocharged form as the J30AC, which powered the now-defunct     Acura TLX Type S and continues to power the MDX Type S via a ten-speed automatic transmission and the brand's Super Handling All-Wheel Drive system, pushing outputs to 355 horsepower and 354 pound-feet of torque. Several parallels can be drawn between Honda's V-6 engineering and Toyota's. Compared to Honda's J-Series V-6, Toyota's 2GR has carved its name in automotive history thanks to overengineered components and high stress limits that not only broaden its performance ceiling but also serve as a durability safety net. Many 2GR-powered vehicles are known to regularly cross 250,000 miles with little more than basic maintenance — a testament to genuine long-term toughness. Many enthusiasts and experts would place the 2GR above the J-Series, and they wouldn't be completely wrong. The 2GR served dutifully across an equally broad range of vehicles as the J-Series — from sedans to pickups, minivans to supercars (see: Lotus Evora). And while the naturally aspirated 2GR was a staple of grunty dependability, it was dropped from the Toyota lineup in favor of the V35A twin-turbo V-6 engine family, which hasn't been as reliable as the 2GR since its debut in the late 2010s. According to Kelley Blue Book, keeping a J30-powered vehicle in peak condition requires strict adherence to its maintenance schedule. The most critical service is the timing belt and water pump replacement, typically recommended every 105,000 miles or seven years. Because this is an interference engine, a belt failure will cause the valves to strike the pistons, leading to catastrophic internal damage. Owners should also perform valve clearance adjustments every 105,000 miles — doing so ensures optimal engine breathing and prevents the ticking noise or burnt valves that can result from neglect. Routine oil changes should occur every 3,000 to 7,500 miles, depending on the oil type used, and transmission fluid replacements every 30,000 miles are standard. A full major service covering the timing belt, water pump, spark plugs, and coolant typically costs between $800 and $1,400, according to data from RepairPal, depending on local labor rates and whether OEM parts are used. While the J30's engine block itself is robust, models produced between 2001 and 2004 that were mated to the five-speed automatic transmission are notorious for overheating and internal clutch failure. On the engine side, common age-related issues include oil leaks from the VTEC spool valve or valve cover gaskets, EGR valve clogging that causes a rough idle, and cracked air intake boots that lead to vacuum leaks and lean engine codes. Of course, no engine is without its faults, and as reliable and proven as the J-Series engine family is, some variants are more renowned than others. Early J30-powered models — including the 1998–2002 Accord V-6, 1999–2003 Acura TL, 1999–2004 Honda Odyssey, and 2003–2008 Honda Pilot — have been reported to have more issues than later variants, including timing belt problems, oil leaks, excessive oil consumption, and occasional fuel injection and electrical quirks. For those shopping for used V-6 Hondas, a professional inspection should always come before any paperwork is signed. Owner forums and discussions on Reddit often point to the transmission as more of a problem area than the engine itself, with numerous owners reporting transmission problems around the 80,000 to 100,000-mile mark. Common issues include: The     modern state of the J-Series engine is characterized by a significant shift away from the traditional single overhead cam layout toward a more complex dual overhead cam configuration. Turbocharging is also a fundamental aspect of the engine's modernization, keeping it alive and relevant today. While the original J30 relied on a belt-driven valvetrain, today's flagship variants, such as the J30AC, adopt a twin-scroll turbocharger and a timing chain to produce more robust power and torque outputs. The latest naturally aspirated 3.5-liter J35Y8 variant powers the 2026 Honda Pilot and 2026 Honda Passport. This powerplant has also transitioned to a DOHC setup, producing 285 horsepower, with direct injection and a Variable Cylinder Management system designed to cut emissions. A ten-speed automatic remains the transmission of choice for these engines, available with either front-wheel drive or an advanced all-wheel drive system. Despite these advancements, the engine family maintains its signature 60-degree V-angle, which Honda insists is best for overall smoothness throughout the rev range. The brand has phased out the traditional VTEC engagement profile on these DOHC heads in favor of continuously variable timing control for more linear and efficient power delivery. Honda is currently facing backlash due to widespread V-6 engine failures among Honda and Acura models. Honda recalled over 200,000 V-6-powered models in 2023 due to a manufacturing defect involving the engine crankshaft, wherein the connecting rod bearings can prematurely wear and seize. Owners report unusual engine noises, misfires, power issues, stalled engines, and hesitation when accelerating. Affected models stretch all the way back to 2014. In January 2026, a lawsuit was filed stating that, despite the recall and subsequent remedy, Honda failed to address the underlying issues. Owners experiencing engine failure well before the 70,000-mile mark are being left to fend for themselves due to lapsed warranties, with some receiving repair quotes in the $10,000-plus range. While not all modern V-6 Honda and Acura models experience this issue, it has been widely reported and should be taken into account before purchasing.
