title: The Balancing Act Starring Melanie Martinez - V Magazine
content: Our digital cover star’s latest projects traverse both heaven and hell on earth. For the artist herself, creation at this level demands total, unbalanced, and obsessive devotion Our digital cover star’s latest projects traverse both heaven and hell on earth. For the artist herself, creation at this level demands total, unbalanced, and obsessive devotion It is sometimes strange to think of Melanie Martinez as a real-life person. Her worlds have always been so vivid, so watertight, so complete, that one forgets they are not places in which she actually lives—forgets, and pictures her instead as an alien who really inhabits these alternate dimensions, the rest of us earthlings watching from the ground, racking up billions of views on her YouTube. Through Cry Baby, K-12, and Portals—the last of which remade her outright as a wide-eyed creature adrift in the afterlife—the character and the woman were nearly impossible to pull apart. It was difficult to picture Melanie Martinez as someone who drives a car, keeps a bank account, scrolls on Instagram, or worries about everyday human things. With HADES, the distance between her invented worlds and ours has begun to collapse. To make an album about hell, Martinez did not have to invent an entire new realm; she only had to look around her—at the homelessness crisis, acute in Los Angeles, where she lives; at cults (including the less obvious ones); at the Disneyfication of girlhood and the young women it strands, each desperate to be a perfect, flawless princess. If the album names the hell around us, the current tour builds it and shuts you in. Night after night, Martinez raises an elaborate underworld onstage—an exaggeration, but one drawn entirely from the world we inhabit (this time, with her). That is the trick of it: the staged hell and the real one are the same hell at different volumes, so exiting the venue doors post-concert only ever turns it down. Which is to say, even after the show ends, concert-goers are still in hell. Just a less fabulous one than the one born from Martinez’s mind. Her artistic surrender—the complete giving-over of the self to the work and world-building—is the animating idea of The Red Shoes, the 1948 film by Michael Powell and Emeric Pressburger, in which a ballerina, possessed by a pair of demonic red slippers, is consumed by her hunger for greatness until it kills her. It became the governing theme of our shoot with Martinez, whom I reached on one of her rare days off, somewhere out on the Hades tour. MATHIAS ROSENZWEIG: I am dying to get into Hades. I’ve been driving around the Portuguese countryside re-listening to the album and really having a moment with it. I wonder what it was like to spend so much time creatively immersed in this album’s darkness. Did writing it ever become a huge bummer, or did it actually feel empowering to harness that darkness into music? MELANIE MARTINEZ: The feelings that came up when writing the album were complex and dynamic, because some days there were real things happening in the world simultaneously as I was writing, and it felt cathartic to be able to shed light on those events. Some days, I’d come into the studio, and I’d be like, “It’s a dark album day.” There’s a dark album and a light album. I was writing both simultaneously. Some days I felt really future-oriented. My mind was in this hopeful place, and it was very light and airy.  Me and [producer] CJ [Baran] would go into the studio Monday through Friday. We treated it like a work schedule. I’d go into the studio at 11 a.m., and I’d leave at midnight or something. We’d make a song every single day, and recorded everything fully. And a lot of the songs—actually every single song that you hear on Hades—were all first-day recordings of my vocals. We didn’t re-record anything. The emotions were complex, but ultimately very cathartic. I’m really proud of the album and that we pushed through all those weird feelings because there were some magical moments as well, like “The Vatican.” I had not known about the crash that happened on Grindr in Milwaukee during the Republican National Convention. I literally was just writing, and then that happened, or we had just found out. I was like, “This could not be more perfect timing.” MR: I was thinking that when someone is younger, their work is naturally more internal. Our internal emotions and feelings are the entire world. With this album—and Portals was definitely a stepping stone—it feels much more external. There is political commentary and social critique alongside more intimate songs like “Possession.” Did you know from the beginning that the album was going to be this meeting ground between your world and the world we live in? MM: I had this intuitive feeling that if I started to write about some dystopian fantasy world, it was gonna reflect in some way—the only influences I have are what’s happening around me. The world does feel very dystopian and scary all the time. It’s constantly flooded with news. You’re scrolling, and you’re like, “Holy shit! This happened, and this happened.” As an artist, you often don’t know what to do with that feeling. You want to be able to express it and make sure you don’t hold it in because it can really affect you. This album naturally leaned in that direction. At a certain point, I got super aware and was like, “Okay, I want to just put down a list of all of the things that I want to talk about.” I love having double meaning and making sure that the titles are all consistent. I love aesthetics, themes, throughline, and story. I was like, “Climate crisis, health systems crisis.” I want to think about all the things I could possibly think of that everyone is collectively witnessing and grieving over. It was very cathartic to do that because afterward you feel such a relief. I don’t know what to do with it other than just express the pain of it, because I think that can be something people will resonate with and hold for themselves. MR: I wanted to bring up “Possession” again, because I know you love double meanings. It made me think about the idea of ownership and intimacy, and especially the term “public figure.” When something is public, there is this implication that it belongs to everyone. I pay taxes; therefore, I have the right to go to the “public park.” For someone in your position, there can be a similar sense that because you are “public,” people somehow have ownership over you. I have always thought it was such a strange term. What do you make of it? MM: I think it is a strange term, but I do think that it’s sadly reflective of how people in the spotlight are treated. There’s so much reflection that I do with that. I journal about it a lot. I try to make sense of it. Painters often get to make art and people look at the art, and that’s the main focus. But with music as a medium, you end up being the focus rather than the music.  A hard thing with being in music is that I feel more like an artist, not like a celebrity. People put that public figure thing on me. It’s strange for me because I don’t resonate with that. It’s a tricky thing to figure out, especially if you’re starting out and all you want to do is make music. It’s really easy for people to go down the path of, “Well, maybe this is what I have to do in order to have my music seen,” or, “Maybe I have to be more in the spotlight, or go to this party, or do this thing, or hang out with this person, or go to this red carpet event.” I think being an introvert naturally has steered me in a direction of being introspective and spending a lot of time alone creating and focusing on the art. I’m grateful for that because I know my nervous system is very sensitive to everything: people, sounds, textures. MR: I’m quite literally interviewing you from a cabin alone in the Portuguese woods, so I understand that sensitivity to surroundings. MM: Exactly. I don’t think my nervous system would be able to handle that lifestyle, and I don’t think it was ever meant for me. But it’s important to talk about when discussing a dystopian world, especially since I am an artist in music. MR: You wanting to do these two sister albums of hell and heaven, it really reminds me of The Divine Comedy. Have you read it? MM: No, but a friend has been trying to get me to. By Danté, right? MM: I don’t know anything about it, but I’ve heard of it, and now that makes me want to. This is also, by the way—I love the alignment of anytime I create something or whatever, and then someone will talk to me about it and their perspective. There are always new things to discover that keep informing the process. It’s a long journey of inspiration, so it’s really exciting having conversations that can just keep it building. MR: How is it going with building the world of your next album, Elysium? Where is the album at the moment? MM: I have one more song. Last minute this year, I decided to replace three songs, and now I’m trying to replace one more. Once Hades was released, I was like, “Okay, now I really want to get to the details of the Utopia and make sure that it’s everything that I want it to be,” because I felt really complete with Hades. Elysium is a harder album for me in general because I’m used to writing about heavier topics and themes. With Elysium, I have to really hone in on a level of hopeful intention for the future of the world, and that can feel really difficult when you’re living in bleak times. With Elysium, there’s no real structure. It’s free-flowing and fluid. I chose to use words that felt light and sweet and airy. I would have a word like “purification.” What does that word mean to me? And then I would write a song that had that energy. It could be something so simple. It was a completely different process for me. The tone of my voice and the sonics are different. It feels like a breath of fresh air, like being in nature, rolling the windows down, and the sun is peeking through. It’s something I’ve never written before. It’s beautiful, and so wholesome, in a way. At the same time, it taps into a deep instinct of the soul. It feels otherworldly while still tapping into human emotion and connection—the more important things in the world—community, any form of togetherness, love. Just basics. MR: Maybe it’s like when I have a really shit day, at the end of the day I try to make a gratitude list and be like, “Okay, everything is really, really tough, but there are still these things, and thank whoever for that.” MM: It’s very much that. All the most important things are the simplest. It’s so different than anything I’ve ever written. I’m excited for people to hear it. With that excitement comes a level of nervousness because I’ve never written anything so light. People are used to hearing me talk about heavy topics. I was like, “Am I going to stay inspired with this album to continue writing it and figuring it out?” I’m still figuring it out. MR: Because your work is so theatrical, do you ever think about expanding into other forms of live performance as a creator? I could even see you doing Marina Abramović-type work. MM: I’m inspired by everything, and I never want to limit myself to different mediums. I can have a spark of inspiration in seconds, and it’ll lead towards some project I never thought I would do. Making a film, even with K-12, I’d never written a script. I was like, “I’m just gonna try.” A lot of what I do comes from a sense of wonderment for the world and art, following your intuition and not second-guessing your instinct to create. It’s a current I try to tap into every day, even though it’s scary sometimes, because you have the world telling you, “You’re not a filmmaker, you don’t know what you’re doing. You didn’t go to school for that.” I do my best to ignore that and follow whatever instinct there is to create, even if it’s with the limited tools I’ve gathered from my life experience. I’m reading a lot of books right now. I’m having such a great time reading. I started writing more, too. It’s been inspiring me to write more journal entries; maybe in the future, I’ll decide to write a book or a weird series. I love that idea that any little thing can inspire you to create a project you never thought you would make. There are endless possibilities. MR: I was listening to an interview you gave recently where you mentioned feeling quite happy lately. What is the correlation between happiness and success for you? MM: My idea of success is the ability to create and make a living from my art. So I’ve never had an idea of external validation dictating what success is. With the success of creating and making a living off of my art, I can help out my family or take care of friends and be there for people in my internal community. I feel really lucky and grateful to be that person for people and to take care of myself and feel stable. My parents grew up in the projects, and I grew up in such a different way from how I’m living now. I’m very aware of where I come from, my family, and how much sacrifice they made for me to do what I love. My mom wanted to do things she loved when she was younger, and she got pushed in a direction for the necessity of making ends meet. She’s very creative, but she didn’t get to express that. So I’m very conscious of that. I’m like, “Okay, my parents sacrificed so much so that I could be able to just create freely,” and it’s a huge deal for me. It makes me emotional, even when I’m around my family. If I talk to my grandmother and hear about her stories, her life, what she’s gone through, I feel such a big responsibility for me to stay grateful and focus on that aspect of success and what that means to me. The way it coincides sometimes or collides with being happy is isolation more than anything. I’m someone who really loves talking to people and connecting. It can be really difficult when you’re leading projects and looked at as the boss in a lot of ways. At the end of the day, I’m a very sensitive, creative person who wants to connect with other like-minded people, but [being in charge] can push you into isolation because they’re like, “You’re the boss.” That aspect plays a role. I do get lonely. That’s the one thing I’m currently working through, even in therapy, trying to understand how I can connect more. MR: That makes so much sense. A musician friend once told me after a big show, “You don’t understand. I go from the crowd and the screams to silence.” She was tearing up telling me that. I joked, “I hosted a perfume launch once,” but of course I couldn’t relate. It must be incredibly isolating because there are only so many people who can fully understand that experience. MM: I don’t really have many artist friends either, so I think that also comes into play. I have my closest friends. I’m so lucky that I’ve been building a solid community of people for 10-plus years. My closest friend is now going on 20-something years of friendship, since we were five. I love that aspect, but it’s also like they [don’t] even know all the time. I’m always talking about, “Oh, I wish that I could really explain to you how weird it is to go on stage and have so much stimulation and people just screaming and yelling.” Your nervous system’s shot; it’s all cortisol. It’s so intense. And then you go back to your hotel, and you’re alone, and you’re in the shower zoning out, and you can hear your ears still ringing. MR: I have one last question for you. I’ve become really obsessed with Stendhal Syndrome where, basically, people would go to Florence and see works of art they’d encountered through iconography their entire lives, and become so overwhelmed by the beauty that they would faint. What piece of art—a painting, a movie, a song, anything—would give you the biggest, almost physical reaction? MM: This is actually gonna sound so silly and really quite stupid, but I’m gonna say it anyway. MM: If I was standing on the fully built practical set of either Edward Scissorhands or The Grinch—wow. I still don’t even understand or comprehend how all of that was practically made. It’s the most inspiring thing to me. I think about that all the time. I’m like, “Fuck the effects. Can we please build it?” MM: Exactly. Yeah. I think that’s probably the thing for me. MR: I love that. You had such a quick response. I’ll bring this up with people, and they’ll come back to me an hour later and be like, “I have it.” And you were like, “No, it’s The Grinch.” MM: It’s been so impactful in my life, and I still come back to it. I love tactile, practically built anything. That’s why I love stop motion movies so much. Have you seen this movie, The Wolf House? A Chilean film. MR: I’ve seen The Wolf House, and I was also looking at the stop-motion artist you had on your Instagram. MM: Yeah, Phoebe [Jane Hart]. She’s so talented. I’m just obsessed with that. Especially now, with AI, it feels more important than ever to keep showing people and the younger generation possibilities of different art forms and different mediums they can tap into because stop motion is such a lost art at this point. You don’t see kids being like, “I want to get into stop motion.” But if I have kids, you best believe I’m gonna be like, “Listen, let’s make some stop motion. title: Cadillac Says This V-One Concept Could Become a Real Car You Can Buy - MotorTrend
content: A personal car based on the V-Series.R Racer? Cadillac says it could happen. Among the tantalizing things Cadillac announced at this year’s Monterey Car Week is the V-One concept you see here. At first glance, the V-One looks a lot like the V-Series.R racing car that Cadillac fields at IMSA and FIA World Endurance Championship races. But the interior is quite the step up from your typical racing-car carbon tub, and the dynamics are meant to be accessible by mere mortals. Is the V-One a future production model? Cadillac was quick to emphasize that this is merely a concept for a track-focused vehicle. That said, it is not a hint at entry into a new racing series, nor something that will be offered for sale to a deep-pocketed racing team. So, is it a future customer car? Cadillac told us that “customer interest will inform future decisions.” Remember that the V-One debuted at the Quail, along with a gorgeous one-off Celestiq and on the heels of the announcement of the “Curated by Cadillac” personalization program. The Quail is where people who can afford specialized roadgoing racers tend to gather. And the people who run Cadillac are not dummies. It sounds like Cadillac could be making a serious come-on to the well-heeled. Power for the V-One concept comes from a V-8-based hybrid drivetrain that delivers 830 horsepower combined, with no finer details except that it “shares its foundations” with the V-Series.R (we assume “foundations” means the 5.5-liter DOHC V-8). Several suspension components are shared with the racing car, including the double-wishbone pushrod-actuated layout. The idea, Cadillac says, is to deliver the racing car’s performance without the driver requiring trained-racing-driver skill. At first glance, the interior might look racing-car spec, what with minimal switches and a steering wheel that looks as much like a smartphone as anything else. However, Cadillac describes the cockpit as—and we’re going to quote directly from the release because, frankly, the words make us salivate—“an intuitive, race-inspired interface and data visualization concept that gives drivers clear feedback and coaching as they explore the car’s full capability.” Did you get what we did from that? Rather than having the computers keep the driver out of trouble, the V-One will (er, could if it gets produced) coach the driver to learn to keep themselves out of trouble. Nice to know there are automakers who don’t necessarily assume self-driving cars are the only future. Cadillac also said that the button layout could be tailored to a client’s specification, as could the driver’s seat. Yes, Cadillac referred to potential buyers as “clients,” same as Ferrari and Rolls-Royce. Curated by Cadillac, indeed. Rich people of the world, you have your assignment: Go tell Cadillac that if it builds a machine like this, you’ll buy it. You will, won’t you? title: Cadillac V-One Concept Previews A Rivalry Against The Wildest Ferraris And McLarens Customers Can Buy - CarBuzz
content: In the last 20 years, automakers have arguably found the limits of what can be done with a road car, and that's led many to shift to making special track-only supercars with hardly any limits on them. That presents a problem: how do you outdo a no-limits track car? The answer some automakers such as Porsche and McLaren have settled on is to turn actual race cars into something for the average rich buyer. Now, Cadillac may join them. Cadillac calls this car the V-One Concept, and it follows the rough formula set by Porsche's one-off 963 RSP for Roger Penske, and the McLaren MCL-HY GTR. It's effectively the LMDh race car that competes in IMSA WeatherTech SportsCar Championship in the US and Canada, and FIA World Endurance Championship overseas, but given the bare minimum of finishing to make it a bit less intimidating and rough for the buyer. It has the same Dallara chassis as the V-Series.R. It has the same pushrod-actuated double-wishbone suspension as the V-Series.R. It only has room for one driver, sits on center-lock wheels, and has the same body as, yes, the V-Series.R. Most importantly, it has the same powertrain, too, a naturally-aspirated 5.5-liter, double-overhead-cam V8 paired with an electric motor. In part because it's still a hybrid, it makes 830 horsepower, 110 more than the McLaren MCL-HY, which ditches the hybrid motor for the private customer vehicle. That's not to say there haven't been any changes. The exterior doesn't have quite as many lights nestled into the front end as the actual race cars. Cadillac also finished it with a gradient paint scheme that was done by hand, and it has unique wheels not shared with the race cars. The interior received the most attention, though. Race car interiors are entirely function over form, and Cadillac put a little effort into sanding down the rough edges. The dashboard has been given a little bit of aesthetic shaping, plus a strip of ambient lighting that's matched at the base of the center console. The single seat has also been spruced up and features upholstery from the Cadillac Collection, which is made from recycled materials. Still, the V-One's cabin is bare bones and remains similar to the race car with a steering yoke complete with telemetry display and controls, and the dash has big, basic buttons. You won't be confusing this for a Celestiq. Cadillac building just one of these V-Ones or even a short run for a few wealthy buyers could just be considered a special opportunity, rather than some indication of the future, since the company knows how to build them and can surely price them to cover the cost. However, Cadillac Executive Design Director Dominic Jajafi had an interesting statement about the concept. "The Cadillac V-ONE Concept is the ultimate manifestation of a customer performance concept and is a clear sign of our ambition for the Cadillac V-Series brand in the future." -Dominic Jajafi, Cadillac Executive Design Director That's a broad statement, and it could go in many directions. We do, though, think it means that we could see more seriously performance-focused models come from Cadillac, particularly inspired by the brand's motorsport programs. Not only does Cadillac participate in endurance racing with the V-Series.R, it just started its first season in Formula 1 this year. As the brand builds its racing reputation, it would only make sense to offer road cars that channel a bit of that mentality. Those cars would probably be more like the Blackwing sedans of late than most of the other V cars that offer some broad handling upgrades, but are mostly high-power GTs than actual sports cars. If you permit us to do a little wishful speculation, we could even see Cadillac creating a car based on the Corvette. It did so before with the XLR convertible, which was effectively a C5 Corvette with a retractable hardtop and a Northstar double-overhead-cam V8. In fact, a version of the Grand Sport X hybrid would be able to claim some similarities to the V-Series.R race car, being a mid-engine V8 hybrid. Just give it Cadillac styling and an extra-luxurious interior, and call it a day. Of course, we want to emphasize we're just daydreaming with this idea, and we'll just have to wait and see what Cadillac actually does. We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful. So you want us to believe Caddy is all about performance while they kill the blackwing? Ok. Not buying it. I see nothing has changed at Cadillac. It’s like Groundhog Day over there. This is the launch of the STS all over again. The caddy that zigs all over again. Dropping the names like fleetwood that made the brand all over again. I don't know....It is probably my over optimistic naivete speaking but after they promised the Cadillac that zigs didn't they produce the CTS V?  And didn't it well zig?  I mean they will not compete with Corvette but maybe a new XLR V to compete with Aston? title: Cadillac’s V-One Concept Refines the Brand’s Pole-Sitting Le Mans Racer - Road & Track
content: The more stately V-One softens up Cadillac’s Le Mans pole-sitter and IMSA champion, the V-Series.R. Whether at Le Mans, Daytona, and a dozen other race tracks across the world, Cadillac’s name is synonymous with an almighty roar. The V-Series.R, the current LMDh-spec racer that Cadillac factory programs run in IMSA GTP and the FIA World Endurance Championship, is a fan favorite in part because of the absurd noise it makes when its naturally-aspirated V-8 bump stops off all-electric power. As of Friday, Cadillac is imagining what that iconic powertrain would look like in a very different context. This is the V-One, the latest Monterey Car Week presentation from Cadillac. It is being called a concept, but Cadillac Executive Design Director Dominic Nafaji also calls it “a clear sign of our ambition for the Cadillac V-Series brand in the future.” Whether or not that means Cadillac actually plans to sell customers a refined version of its V-One, it feels like a good sign that the brand imagines more naturally-aspirated track cars going forward in one way or another. Aside from a unique two-tone finish of silver and dark blue, the exterior of the V-One should look extremely familiar to anyone who has seen the V-Series.R on track. The V-One even carries a low-mounted rear wing, a hallmark of the V-Series.R only since its aerodynamic platform was updated for the start of the 2026 IMSA season. Everything else, from the massive fin on the back of the engine cover to the flying buttress-like winglets attached only to the inside of all four fenders, carries over from the race car. Things turn more unique inside, where Cadillac has followed Porsche’s one-off 963 RSP by refining the sharp edges of the spartan cabin of what would otherwise be a race car. Softer materials, including recycled fabrics, cover some of the hard carbon fiber surfaces someone might expect to find on a race car. A steering wheel specific to the V-One sits at the center, running what Cadillac calls “an intuitive, race-inspired interface and data visualization concept.” In other words, the car’s user interface has also been adjusted to be more accommodating to potential private owners. Performance comes from that familiar 5.5-liter V-8 as part of a hybrid powertrain, producing a combined 830 horsepower in this application. Suspension components are shared with the race car, as well. To be sure, the V-One is not exactly a V-Series.R road car, even in concept form. Instead, this is best thought of as Cadillac’s slightly more plush answer to the Ferrari 499P Modificata or the Aston Martin Valkyrie LM—a variant of a Le Mans racer built with a customer in mind. Even that is still theoretical, though. This is just a concept for now, one debuting at The Quail, a Motorsports Gathering as part of Monterey Car Week. We’ll have to wait to see if Cadillac has anything more planned for this particular evolution of its race-winning prototype. See more photos of the Cadillac V-One Concept here. Fred Smith's love of cars comes from his fascination with auto racing. Unfortunately, that passion led him to daily drive a high-mileage, first-year Porsche Panamera. He is still thinking about the last lap of the 2011 Indianapolis 500. We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we back.

title: Kian v. Florida : The Right to Be Tried Before a Twelve-Person Jury - Cato Institute
content: Sign up to have blog posts delivered straight to your inbox! When Hamed Kian was charged in Florida with five counts of practicing chiropractic medicine with a suspended license—a felony carrying up to five years in prison—he was tried before a six-person jury. Convicted on all counts by this truncated panel, Mr. Kian appealed, arguing that Florida’s six-person jury rule deprived him of his right to a trial by a twelve-person jury as required by the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments. The Florida appellate court affirmed his conviction without a written opinion, and Mr. Kian asked the US Supreme Court to review his case. In trying felony cases before six-person juries, Florida’s reliance on the Supreme Court’s 1970 decision in Williams v. Florida breaks from centuries of tradition. The Framers incorporated the common-law criminal jury into Article III and the Sixth Amendment as a vital structural check against government overreach, overzealous prosecution, and judicial bias. While the Constitution’s text does not explicitly specify a numerical requirement, the Court’s recent originalist jurisprudence—most notably in Ramos v. Louisiana—reaffirms that the Sixth Amendment protects the fundamental attributes the criminal jury possessed at common law. Historically, the requirement that a criminal petit jury consist of precisely twelve members remained undisputed in English and American law for hundreds of years until Williams improperly abandoned that historical scope. The Supreme Court granted Mr. Kian’s petition, and the Cato Institute filed an amicus brief in support of Mr. Kian. In our brief, we ask the justices to overrule Williams v. Florida and reverse the decision. Our brief stresses that the structural guarantees of the Bill of Rights cannot be subjected to arbitrary judicial interest-balancing or functionalist reduction. Restoring the common law twelve-person jury requirement is essential to protecting defendants’ constitutional rights, maintaining public confidence in judicial outcomes, and upholding the original meaning of the Sixth Amendment. title: A Conversation with Poetic V - Poetry Center
content:
Some voices don’t just write poetry; they carry it, live it, and use it to heal others in the process. Vanessa Williams, known as “Poetic V,” is a California-raised, Las Vegas-based poet, teacher, spoken word artist, and author whose work is rooted in truth, faith, and transformation. With more than ten poetry slam wins, performances across eight states, and stages including TEDx, South by Southwest, and the Las Vegas Book Festival, she has built a powerful presence that extends far beyond the mic. Through her writing and her book Poetically Affirmed, she uses her own life experiences to give voice to the voiceless and remind others that even grief has purpose, and healing is always within reach. Can you share a bit about your journey as a poet—what drew you to poetry and how your craft has evolved? My poetry journey began at the age of 10 in my 5th-grade writing class. The assignment was to write a poem about “Home.” Before this moment, I had never written a poem, so I was a bit nervous. An A+ and framed poem hanging in my room like an award later, something in me “clicked.” I found myself writing all the time. Short stories, poems, free writes, etc. In a home where emotions and feelings were prisoners, I found freedom in pen and paper. A year later, I joined a Performing Arts Ministry Group called Tribe of Judah World Outreach, where we traveled all over the world telling people about God through dance, step routines, and POETRY! I was able to encourage and help others through my experiences. In 2017, my mother passed away, and poetry shifted again. Tears filled pages more than words did, and I was reminded of how much I need to write. Understanding how important it is to release what is inside in order to really heal. In 2018, I moved to Las Vegas from Southern California, where I was introduced to poetry again. Not just for therapy or helping others, but also as a career. I get paid for this now! Lol. But in all seriousness, there's nothing like getting paid for something you love to do. In April 2021, I wrote and published my first book, “Poetically Affirmed”: A collection of ‘I Am’ poems to affirm you daily. I was dealing with so many emotions and I knew I wanted to be better than I was, so I wrote myself into the place I wanted to be. My poetry continues to evolve as I do, and sometimes before me. As if I am catching up to the poems. What poets make up your "literary family tree"? In other words, which poets or poems have been most meaningful to you as a writer of poetry? My literary family tree includes poets like Patricia Smith, Ebony Stewart, Rudy Francisco, Maya Angelou, and Ariana Brown. What draws me to each of them is their ability to tell the truth with both vulnerability and strength—to write in a way that moves people long after the poem ends. What does your writing process look like? Are there inspirations or experiences that guide your poetry? My writing process happens in two ways. One, getting a lightning stick of inspiration from something I've heard or seen, and I have to immediately write it out. Or two, having a topic I am passionate about and making time to write. I have fallen in love with editing. For a long time, I would never edit my poems. However they came out, that's what it was. Wild! I know. But now, I see how a poem really comes alive as it's dissected. Most of my writing comes from life experiences. Not to sound corny, but my life is my inspiration. From faith to love to women's rights, injustice among the black community, etc. It all comes from my heart to the ears and eyes of whoever is willing to listen and read. I know if I am facing something, someone else is as well, so let me write to uplift us both. Which of your works do you feel most deeply represents your voice, and what themes or messages are central to your poetry? I have a poem entitled “Eulogy for the Living.” It is so easy to only focus on what we have lost, who has left us, and where the holes are. But I realized in doing this, we miss who and what are still standing next to us. This poem is a thank you to my father and represents the raw emotions of grief, while not making it an idol where nothing else matters. Going through this, my faith was and still is being tested. I realized how little grief is talked about in Church. Or when it is talked about, it's met with a “just pray on it, you'll be alright.” But what happens when sorrow sucks the life out of you, and you can’t pray? I wasn't alright, and I wasn’t going to pretend. I began to write the truth about grief and faith. Telling the truth and giving hope. This has become the main focus of my poetry and ties in so many other topics such as identity, value, world views, etc. Are there recurring symbols, metaphors, or motifs that continue to appear across your body of work? What draws you back to them? I often use ocean or water metaphors. When it comes to the ocean, I love its duality. Calm yet can cause chaos. Can birth and destroy life. It is my favorite place on earth. My mom used to call me a ‘fish’ because once I was in that water, I wasn't coming out. We had that in common. Once she passed, her ashes were spread in the ocean, so now it's the place I feel most close to her. Water reminds me of the Holy Spirit, and many times in spiritual texts, his characteristics are those of water. How intentionally do you build visual landscapes within your poetry? For a long time, I just wrote. Whatever I felt, that was it. Didn’t even edit most of the time. I know; blasphemy. But now I want people to see the poem, not just hear it, and visuals make emotions tangible. If I’m talking about heartbreak, I don’t just want the audience to understand pain — I want them to feel like they’re standing inside the room where it happened. Imagery for me is one of the biggest parts of my writing process now. I think in scenes first. It’s like a movie. I often ask myself, “What does this emotion look like, sound like, smell like?” before I write. Whether it’s comparing grief to a cracked bone healing wrong or faith to being held underwater and still breathing, I use visual language to make abstract emotions easier to connect to. How do music, culture, memory, or personal history influence the texture and tone of your poetry? Music, culture, memory, and personal history shape every poem I write. I grew up understanding that stories carry power, and poetry became the place where my experiences, my faith, and my community could all meet. The rhythm of spoken word, gospel, and everyday conversations all find their way into my work. I don’t write just to tell my story—I write so someone else can find themselves in it. My poetry is rooted in healing, restoration, and purpose. Every piece is an opportunity to turn memory into meaning and remind people that even the hardest chapters can become part of a greater testimony. Is there a particular poem in your collection that challenged you technically or emotionally? What made it difficult to complete? I am currently writing a poem called “Who Told You God was White?” I’m very passionate about using my poetry to lead people to God, or at least curious enough to listen to the whole poem. This piece is so important to me because the narrative in most people's minds is that Christianity is a white man’s religion used as a weapon for manipulation and control. But that’s just not the truth. My desire with this piece is to provide factual information and evidence, while expressing God's heart for all. I want to be sensitive yet bold, truthful yet tactful. I’m excited and nervous. As a Black woman poet, how have you navigated visibility and recognition in the literary world? Have there been specific challenges or breakthroughs? Living in a city like Las Vegas, visibility and recognition as a black poet have actually been attainable. I truly believe this is because of so many black poets before me and the work they have done. When it comes to academia and publishing outside of Vegas, however, the hurdles are there. In 2024, only 5-6% of authors are black, and even a smaller number of those writers are poets. This is why articles like this are so important. We must be encouraged to write, submit, and publish despite rejection. And this has been my stance for years. The world will see and hear us whether they like it or not. How do you see your work contributing to broader conversations about Black identity, womanhood, or contemporary culture? My work contributes to these conversations because it unveils another side of the stories already being told. Like another patch in a quilt of black importance, my work brings comfort, warmth, and value to all who experience it, especially when it comes to black women and grief. There is such a notion that the black woman must always remain strong, in control, never tired or weary. But the truth is “Black Women Grieve.” My work gives a voice to those who are too busy or ashamed to speak. How has building relationships within literary communities or collaborating with other artists shaped your work and career? I owe 90% of my career to connecting with communities and collaborating with other artists. Before coming to Vegas, I never knew any of this was possible. Now the possibilities are endless. So many of the features, shows, and opportunities I have been awarded come from a connection or someone mentioning my name when I wasn't in the room. The way we are able to come together, learn from one another, and expand the reach of poetry is a poem all by itself. I have learned the power of connection and truly believe we were never meant to do this on our own. What makes a powerful slam poem? What makes slam different from poetry on the page? When I think of Slam poetry, I think of written poetry coming alive. It is no longer words echoed in your own voice as you read, but it has hands, feet, and a heartbeat you cannot ignore. Slam poetry gives the written words, without sounding cliché, a voice. It allows the poet to explore different tones and expressions of a poem. Experimenting with character and even adding theatrical elements. To me, slam poetry takes the limits off the artist. What guidance would you give to emerging Black women poets who are trying to find their voice, gain visibility, and make an impact in today’s literary landscape? First thing you must know beyond any doubt that would try to speak to you, whether inward or outward, your story is needed! There are hundreds of black women poets, but God only created one you. Secondly, gaining inspiration from other poets is vital and powerful, but do not think you must sound or write like others to be accepted or seen. The world needs your authenticity. Thirdly, become a master at this craft. Never stop learning, growing, and perfecting. And lastly, have fun! Remember why you write. Enjoy the journey and know somebody is being changed by your vulnerability! Vanessa Williams AKA “Poetic V” is a California raised, Las Vegas living Poet, teacher, spoken word artist and author. She has won over 10 poetry slams and has written and published her own poetry book Poetically Affirmed. Poetic V has had the privilege of being a featured artist in over 8 states and 30+ events, including the Las Vegas Book Festival, Miss Nevada African Pageant, 3x Utah Arts Festival performer, South by South West performer and a Tedx presenter. Lillie Mae is a Brand Strategist, media contributor, and visibility expert dedicated to helping women elevate their voice, brand, and influence. She has been featured as a contributor to Sheen Magazine, Rolling Out Magazine, HelloBeautiful.com, BlackLove.com, and more, using storytelling and strategic media to amplify impactful narratives. Through her platform and membership at HerVisibility.com, she creates opportunities for women leaders and creatives to expand their reach through podcast interviews, speaking engagements, and brand exposure. Connect with her on Instagram at Instagram.com/iamLillieMae. College of Humanities

title: Understanding the court’s next major case on asylum seekers: Wassily v. Blanche - SCOTUSblog
content: This coming term, in Wassily v. Blanche, the Supreme Court will decide whether asylum beneficiaries are barred from obtaining lawful permanent residency if their asylum status has been terminated. Wassily is of considerable significance. While the termination of asylum status once was relatively uncommon, recent policy changes by the Trump administration have exposed far more immigrants to the risk of this. The legal dispute in Wassily, which has divided the federal courts, dates back to unclear language in the Refugee Act of 1980. The Refugee Act laid the framework for the modern asylum system and defined legal standards for asylum officers, immigration judges, and other immigration adjudicators. The act used precise, detailed language in crafting the refugee process for noncitizens outside of the United States, but Congress left internal asylum procedures more undefined, with less statutory guidance. Over time, asylum claims increased dramatically, making unclear statutory gaps more and more troublesome. Indeed, that lack of statutory clarity is front and center in Wassily. The Refugee Act specified that refugees processed outside the United States could only obtain a permanent resident green card if their refugee “admission has not been terminated.” By contrast, the act was unclear whether that same requirement also applied to asylees who had obtained asylum status from within the United States. For asylees applying to “adjust” to permanent resident status, as codified at 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b), the Refugee Act did not mention termination at all. Instead, the act only said that the immigration official “may” grant the green card for “any alien granted asylum” who met the admissibility requirements. The act did not say whether “granted asylum” meant anyone who previously had been granted asylum or whether that phrase was limited to those with a current asylum status. Tamer Wassily left his native Egypt and entered the United States in 1993. He was granted asylum in 2000 based on his claim of persecution in Egypt as a Coptic Christian. Later, he was convicted of stalking and child endangerment, at which point the DHS sought to terminate his asylum status before an immigration judge. The immigration judge agreed and terminated this based on the finding that Wassily’s stalking conviction was a “particularly serious crime.” But the immigration judge found him eligible to adjust to a green card because the immigration statute did not contain “an explicit requirement” of current asylum status. Byron Velasquez Arreaga entered the United States in 1995 and was granted asylum. He later was convicted of multiple crimes for driving while intoxicated. The DHS sought to terminate his asylum status and scheduled an immigration court hearing. The immigration judge terminated his asylum status for particularly serious crimes. In contrast to Wassily’s immigration judge, this immigration judge found that without a current asylum status, Velasquez Arreaga could not adjust status to a green card and he was ordered removed to his native country of Guatemala. The parties appealed both cases. The Board of Immigration Appeals weighed in on the statutory confusion in a precedent decision: Matter of T-C-A-. The BIA interpreted the statute as meaning that only a noncitizen with current asylum status could adjust to permanent resident status. In Wassily’s appeal, the BIA relied on Matter of T-C-A-. It found that Wassily’s terminated asylum status made him ineligible for adjustment to a green card. The BIA also found Velasquez Arreaga ineligible for adjustment. In tandem cases for Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga, a divided panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit agreed with the majority of circuits that only noncitizens with current asylum status were eligible for asylee adjustment. The 2nd Circuit concluded that the statutory phrase “granted asylum” was best understood to require a current asylum “status” – a legally significant term as used by Congress. The panel majority said its reading was “buttressed” by statutory context, including the Immigration Act of 1990. That act explicitly created a time-restricted exception that allowed some noncitizens to apply for green cards “regardless of whether or not such asylum has been terminated.” The circuit reasoned that this limited exception, as a “statutory note,” did not create a general rule that noncitizens could apply for permanent residency after termination. In dissent, Judge Beth Robinson adopted the minority view of the circuits on this “difficult” statutory question. She reasoned that the asylee adjustment statute meant that “any” noncitizen was eligible to adjust who previously had been granted asylum. Under Robinson’s view, the absence of the word “status” from the statutory provision must have been an intentional omission by Congress. The Supreme Court granted certiorari in June to review the statutory question of whether terminated asylees are eligible to apply for adjustment to permanent residency. In their petition for certiorari, Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga argue that the statutory text and context are clear that any noncitizen who was “granted asylum” previously can seek permanent residence after termination. They interpret “granted” as a past tense verb, and they contend that the omission of “status” in the statutory language must be given effect because Congress knew how to include such a requirement. As broader statutory context, Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga emphasize the adjacent Section 1159(c), which allows for a discretionary “waiver” of other requirements for the noncitizen’s admissibility. According to them, it would be “strange” to interpret the statute as “categorically” stripping the attorney general of that discretionary authority where the asylee’s status has been terminated. Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga also invoke the rule of lenity – the canon that a statutory ambiguity should be construed in favor of the noncitizen. They claim that lenity is especially paramount after the Supreme Court’s 2024 decision in Loper Bright v. Raimondo, which eliminated the doctrine of Chevron deference to a federal agency’s (here, the BIA’s) reasonable interpretation of an ambiguous statute. In an atypical move where only the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 2nd, 4th, and 5th Circuits so far have looked at this issue, Solicitor General D. John Sauer agrees that the Supreme Court should grant review. Even so, the solicitor general maintains that the 2nd Circuit was correct in interpreting asylee adjustment as limited to noncitizens with current asylum status. The government says that Congress’ intent is best understood as giving effect to the termination of asylum “status” as a bar to obtaining a green card. The solicitor general relies on the statutory note in the Immigration Act of 1990 as evidence that Congress only excepted a small subset of asylees from the general rule barring terminated asylees from adjustment of status. Without citing Loper Bright, the government disputes that the rule of lenity is applicable here at all. The solicitor general argues that the discretionary waiver at Section 1159(c) does not undermine the most natural reading of asylee adjustment because “the decision to terminate is itself discretionary” and the court should give effect to that waiver authority. The Supreme Court’s resolution of this case could impact the interests of the millions of asylum applicants with cases pending in the immigration courts and asylum offices, as well as those persons granted asylum status in recent years. Even if the Supreme Court narrowly frames this case as a discrete statutory question, it will clarify the effect of the government’s termination authority for anyone granted asylum. This is especially timely: in December 2025, the DHS announced that it would “comprehensively re-review” asylum approvals from “high-risk” countries since entry in 2021. At the end of that review, the DHS could elect to terminate asylum status. In June 2026, a federal district court vacated the DHS re-review policy, but the government is challenging that ruling. That’s not all. The case also could have broader implications for federal administrative law if the justices take an interest in the parties’ arguments about the government’s discretionary authority or Loper Bright. The Supreme Court has not yet relied on Loper Bright in deciding an immigration case. In fairness, the 2nd Circuit found no need to do so, and the Supreme Court avoided a similar issue in Urias-Orellana v. Bondi, a case that concerned the judicial standard of review for asylum “persecution” determinations. But that does not mean the court will continue to let this issue linger. Disclosure: When he was at the DOJ, the author litigated Wassily before the 2nd Circuit. He no longer has any involvement in the case or its litigation before the Supreme Court. Duncan Fulton is an Assistant Professor at Loyola University New Orleans College of Law. He has litigated more than 100 immigration cases in federal courts nationwide. title: Coach V’s Corner: I’ve Never Seen a Woodchuck - Post Independent
content: It has to be well over 30 years now that I received a call late on an August Friday night from my friend and running buddy Bob Willey. He wanted to know if I would join him the following morning for a new 5-mile race at Rifle Falls State Park called the Cheatin’ Woodchuck Chase. After immediately declining his invite, I wondered out loud if race directors would release a large group of varmints in the park, with adult human varmints in hot pursuit. Whoever catches the first one wins, or loses, depending on the temperament of that particular woodchuck. It seemed silly. After much cajoling from Willey, with a few guilt trips thrown in for good measure, I agreed to go on what was sure to be a foolhardy adventure. An adventure it turned out to be, indeed. After picking me up bright and early, Willey’s dilapidated old Audi decided to start shaking and belching smoke on Interstate 70 just west of New Castle. When the rattling and rusty old relic finally made it clear of traffic and safely to the side of the road, all I could think of to say was, “Well, at least we weren’t in an airplane!” With hopes of chasing elusive woodchucks now completely dashed, Willey and I got on U.S. 6 and 24 and jogged back to New Castle, stopping at Mattivi’s gas station. As luck would have it, a tow truck and a driver were right there on site. I had never ridden in one, but it was quite a treat hitching up the car and getting a tow back to Glenwood Springs in the big rig, with Willey giving the driver an earful about our misbegotten morning the entire way. Not to be denied, the following year, we jumped into a much more reliable vehicle and made it to the race. In the many years that have followed our abbreviated initial attempt, I have made it to more Woodchuck Chases than I can count, but I have yet to see an actual woodchuck! I’ll give it another shot this year on Saturday, Aug. 22. Sponsored once again by Rifle Recreation, the race is now a 5K and will begin and end near the Rifle State Fish Hatchery. The format is a little different this year, with runners going up the road from the hatchery for 1.55 miles and then retracing their steps back down. Start time is 9 a.m., and full details can be found at the EcoPoint Race Series on the Rifle Recreation website. Don’t forget about Saturday’s Dog Day 5K at Two Rivers Park in Glenwood Springs. The Aug. 15 run starts and finishes near the bandshell and is out and back on the Rio Grande Trail. The start time is 9 a.m., and all proceeds will benefit Colorado Animal Rescue. When I saw that Roaring Fork High School would once again field a varsity football team at the 1A level, I was reminded of all the great rivalry games between the Rams and the Glenwood Demons back when I was in high school in the late 1970s. The game between the two undefeated Northwestern League leaders in the late fall of 1978 is still the best game, with the biggest crowd I have ever witnessed at Glenwood’s stadium. It wasn’t called Stubler Memorial Field at the time because Coach Stubler was still a legend in the making as one of the assistant football coaches for the Demons. Glenwood and coach Don Miller went on to win that hard-fought game against the Rams and capture the 2A state championship a few months later on a snowy December Saturday in Glenwood Springs that was better suited for penguins than football players and fans. I wish Coach John Nielsen and the Rams the very best of luck this fall. The first game is at home in Carbondale on Friday night, Aug. 21, against Gunnison, with a 7 p.m. kickoff. I will get up to Carbondale for a few games and also catch some of the Demons this fall at what is now Stubler Memorial Field. title: Grand Theft Column V - The Daily Tar Heel
content: This week, I write that violent video games make people violent. It’s gonna be easy. Just throw together a few words scolding people who play them, maybe get a professional to back me up and you’ll be on your way to reading the kvetches before you can even say, “He phoned this one in.” Tuesday at midnight, stores released the newest in one of the most violent and popular video game series ever made, “Grand Theft Auto V.” The GameStop on Franklin Street had a swarm of college kids lined up. They’re saying it has new levels of drugs, robberies, heinous crime … and that’s just Franklin Street. (Ba dum bum.) I looked at the people in line with suspicion. With times becoming more and more violent, was I looking at future killers? I know firsthand how games can negatively impact you. I grew up playing “GoldenEye 007” in the ’90s. I spent hours playing it, becoming more and more desensitized. To this day, I still go into a karate-chopping blackout anytime I see a Russian. I spoke via telephone with James Ivory, an associate professor at Virginia Tech’s department of communication who has researched the effects of violent video games. He’d tell me what I needed to hear. “There’s very little evidence to correlate video games with serious violent crime,” Ivory said. Yes, just as I had always susp- … wait, what? Very little evidence? I could barely contain my game-playing-induced rage. After slamming down the phone and hitting it repeatedly with a bat, I decided to play the new game for myself to prove once and for all, if I spent enough time playing PS3, I could finally intimidate someone physically. In the new game, one of the main characters, Trevor, is like a meth head Tamagotchi, whom you can make do unspeakably violent things. You can even make him huff gas. The truth is … I loved it! And in real life, I’m a normal, well-adjusted gas-huffer who would never dream of acting out violently. I guess what I’m saying is, when it comes to games, we’re less like sponges, and more like … well, giant impenetrable blobs. So, if there’s very little evidence of a correlation between video games and real-life violent behavior, why does that seem like the opposite of common knowledge? I suspect most people don’t want to get to the real causes. If young people are getting more violent, video games may be a symptom, but these new parents are definitely the disease. I mean, the Greeks didn’t worry their kids would come home from “Oedipus” and gouge each other’s eyes out. They trusted them to do it because it was the honorable thing. I guess what I’m saying is, if we all band together … (nervous, sweating) … um, everything in moderation … dinners as families … (Takes out, fires gun in air) EVERYONE DOWN, THIS IS A ROBBERY!

title: Once upon a time: storytelling in Learning Resources v. Trump - SCOTUSblog
content: Every fall, with each new class of 1Ls, we legal writing teachers undertake a strange job. We spend an entire year trying to get students to not write like lawyers, a notoriously dreadful category of writers. In pursuit of that goal, we often target the bad qualities like jargon, legalese, word-wasting phrases, and other legal idiosyncrasies. But I think we’d get better results if we started with what makes any writing “good” – whether it is written by lawyers or by actual humans. As evidence, I would point to the Supreme Court’s best writers, who deploy tactics often taught (and missed) in a good English composition class. Take Chief Justice John Roberts as an example. Flash back to November 2025: if you’re Roberts, you’ve got a problem – or at least a challenge. You’ve just assigned yourself the majority opinion in Learning Resources v. Trump. Now you must convince readers inside and outside the court that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act provides no authority for the one policy most important to this president: tariffs. Never mind that the solicitor general has warned that your decision will provoke another Great Depression. Never mind that the outcome depends upon Talmudic esoterica unfamiliar to a politicized public – things like separation of powers, textualism, and the major questions doctrine. Beyond all that, you must communicate dreadful source material, especially to non-legal readers. Those readers must learn something of IEEPA itself, which clocks in at around 2,000 words of abstract text. Then, they need the content of the president’s orders, which add almost 12,000 words, even without the appendices. Roberts solves this problem by meeting the expectations of the ordinary, English-language reader. Apart from citations, he tells a 422-word story, and he does it with a tactic any writer can emulate: He uses actors as the subjects of most of his sentences. In a conflict over presidential power, Roberts makes the president the main character in a story, both in setting out IEEPA’s requirements and in summarizing the president’s orders. After an initial topic sentence about IEEPA, he puts the president – rather than the statute – in the subject position. He writes that, to satisfy IEEPA, “the President must identify” a threat. Then, “he must declare” an emergency. Then “he” may “regulate [. . . 16 words later . . .] importation.” Turning to the facts, the chief keeps the president – rather than his orders – in the spotlight. He practically ties the president to a chair at center stage. In the narrative, “President Trump sought” to address two, specific threats (“The first was the influx of illegal drugs from Canada, Mexico, and China,” and “[t]he second was ‘large and persistent’ trade deficits.”). Roberts writes that the “President determined” the threats were serious. “He invoked” his power under IEEPA. As required by the statute, “President Trump declared” the requisite emergency. “He then imposed” tariffs, which “the President” later changed when “he increased” or “he removed” tariffs. Later, “the President . . . shifted . . . goods into and out of” the tariff regime. Indeed, in all the sentences he wrote for Section I.A of the opinion, the chief used an actor as the subject in all but five. In making that choice, the chief is not employing some tactic unique to “legal” writing, separate from ordinary English prose. Your old English composition teacher has long known the power of storytelling language. One such teacher, Joseph Willams, changed the way I wrote as a lawyer, and I love the way he put it. In the book Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace, he focuses on what every reader needs from a writer. While readers look for action in the verbs, “they want characters as subjects even more.” You erect tripping hazards for your reader when, “for no good reason,” you “fail to name characters in subjects, or worse, delete them entirely.” Unfortunately, most lawyers don’t write this way. Most lawyers – even great ones – write more like the Congressional Research Service. In its September 2025 report on IEEPA, CRS covers essentially the same ground as the chief’s 422-word story. But instead of a story, CRS offers up a report filled with tripping hazards. It force-feeds the reader five dense pages (10–14) of abstract prose, replete with footnotes. Where Roberts describes IEEPA by focusing on the president, CRS hangs a 56-word sentence on “IEEPA empowers.” Readers must then swallow a 50-word sentence hung on “statute provides.” And the public is reminded that each “new threat . . . requires” certain actions by the president. The coup de grace? CRS treats readers to a dreadful block quote of IEEPA’s central provisions. To be sure, the president does appear in the paragraphs discussing the tariff orders. But if Roberts ties the president to a chair, CRS permits him to wander on and off stage. In the president’s absence, readers must content themselves with massive sentences about the “January Proclamation” or the “February Executive Orders.” Again, rather than a story, the reader must shoulder a bureaucratic tome – scrupulously accurate, no doubt, but abstract enough and long enough to avoid being read at all. The chief, in contrast, uses storytelling both to be read and to be understood, all while setting up his version of the question. Remember the story: The president issued barely related tariffs that swallowed the entire economy, then he changed them at random. But Congress wrote, “regulate . . . [yadda, yadda, yadda] . . . importation.” Based on this language, can a president really set tariffs “on imports from any country, of any product, at any rate, for any amount of time”? So, how to write like the chief rather than like a lawyer? Prefer actors as subjects rather than concepts or abstractions like proclamations, orders, tariffs, separation of powers, or the major questions doctrine. Of course, “prefer” means you’ll occasionally discover “good reason” to abandon this approach, but not nearly as often as you think. For the moment, create drafts like you always do, then build in storytelling when you line edit. In the end, good legal writers do the same things as good writers in any field. Good writers tell stories where characters do things. And here, the president was doing things, but without a permission slip from congress. title: BTS star V reveals hearing loss battle during livestream - BBC
content: V, a member of pop sensation BTS, says he has been receiving treatment for hearing loss in one ear, an announcement that comes midway through the band's highly-anticipated world tour. In a livestream on Wednesday, the 30-year-old said that he has dealt with the problem for about two and a half years. This was the first time he was revealing it to the band's fans, he said. "If the hearing in my left ear is at 100, it's only about 30 in my right," said V, whose real name is Kim Tae-hyung. The band is currently on its first world tour in years, marking the reunion of all seven members since they went on a hiatus for mandatory military service. During the livestream, V said his hearing became worse when he was serving in the military. But he said he did not take it seriously at first, believing it to be "a matter of mental strength". He added he was now taking medication and going to hospital regularly. With rare exceptions, all able-bodied men are required to serve 18 months of military service in South Korea. This included BTS members, who were at the height of their fame in 2022 when they started taking career breaks to enlist in the military. V joined the military in 2023 and was discharged in June 2025. The Arirang World Tour, which kicked off in April in South Korea, marked the highly-anticipated reunion of the band's seven members. The livestream on Wednesday came after the band wrapped its concerts in Baltimore, Maryland. V was joined by his bandmate Jungkook, who talked about a shin injury he has been dealing with during the tour, saying he was "on the verge of developing a stress fracture". Jungkook added that he would have to manage his injury well in order to keep performing. In the coming months, the concert tour will take BTS to cities around the world, including Los Angeles, Buenos Aires, Bangkok, Sydney and Hong Kong. A search and rescue operation is under way to find survivors in Flores, an island in eastern Indonesia.
